title: Full Light
summary: Having slipped through the loose bar of the Rue Plumet gate, Marius spends every evening of May 1832 in the garden with Cosette. Their love is chaste to the point of innocence: a first kiss that is also the last, hands held, nonsense talked, and the discovery that her real name is Euphrasie.
details: The narrator fills in what the reader has guessed: Éponine, having recognised through the gate who lived in the Rue Plumet, first kept the ruffians away and then led Marius there, and after days of ecstasy outside the railing he forced one of the rusty bars and entered the garden as Romeo entered Juliet's. Since the street is always empty and he comes only at night, no one sees him. From the evening of their first kiss he is there every night.

Hugo insists on the purity of what follows. Through the whole month of May the two sit in the neglected, fragrant garden and adore each other without crossing any line they are even aware of; Marius kisses her hand or a lock of hair and no more, and once turns his eyes away when her bodice slips. They have begun to call each other thou. Cosette confides that her real name is Euphrasie and that Cosette was a childhood nickname, then decides she prefers Cosette after all because he does. Marius confesses he once thought her name was Ursule, which makes them laugh all evening; he starts to mention the day he nearly fought a veteran at the Luxembourg and stops, since that would mean speaking of her garter.

Marius imagines life as nothing more than this: coming every evening, moving the bar, sitting elbow to elbow on the bench, calling her thou, smelling the same flower. His compliments are lyrical and shy; she answers that she has loved him a little more every hour since morning. Cosette, fresh from the convent, talks with surprising good sense; both weep over a crushed ladybird and laugh like two boys. The chapter closes on the two lovers whispering in the dark while the planets wheel overhead.

title: The Bewilderment of Perfect Happiness
summary: The lovers exist in a daze, unaware even of the cholera ravaging Paris. They have exchanged their names and little else: Marius has forgotten to tell Cosette about the Gorbeau ambush and her father's strange flight, and neither asks where any of this is leading.
details: Marius and Cosette do not notice the cholera decimating Paris that very month. They have confided in each other, but only as far as names and outlines. Marius has said he is an orphan named Marius Pontmercy, a lawyer who lives by writing for publishers, the son of a colonel who was a hero, on bad terms with a rich grandfather; he hinted at being a baron, a word Cosette does not understand. She has told him she was brought up at the Petit-Picpus convent, that her mother is dead like his, that her father is M. Fauchelevent, very good, generous to the poor and poor himself.

Strangely, the recent past has gone so hazy for Marius that this satisfies him entirely. It never occurs to him to tell Cosette about the night in the Jondrette garret, about Thénardier, the burn, or the odd behaviour and flight of her father. In the evening he hardly remembers the morning. The two live only in the hours they are together, somnambulists who have told each other everything except everything.

Hugo describes them suspended between earth and heaven, hardly flesh and blood, with no yesterday or tomorrow. Marius sometimes closes his eyes in her presence to see her soul better. Neither of them asks where this is to lead; they consider that they have already arrived.

title: The Beginning of Shadow
summary: Jean Valjean suspects nothing of the nightly visits, and Toussaint sleeps through them; only Courfeyrac notices Marius coming home at one in the morning and fails to get a name out of him. Then one evening, at the corner of the Rue Plumet, Éponine stops Marius with a greeting he answers awkwardly, and she leaves abruptly after failing to find words.
details: Cosette's gaiety is enough to keep Jean Valjean content, and the small habitual precautions of lovers keep him blind. She agrees to every proposal he makes; since he goes to bed at ten, Marius comes only after that hour, when he hears Cosette open the glass door onto the veranda. Valjean has stopped thinking that Marius exists, though one morning he remarks that Cosette has whitewash on her back, from being pushed against the wall the night before. Toussaint, who retires early, knows nothing either. Marius never enters the house; the two sit in a recess by the steps, and he always sets the bar of the gate back so no displacement shows.

He returns to Courfeyrac's lodgings around midnight. Courfeyrac, a practical man, is impatient with this invisible paradise, tells Marius he is getting irregular in his habits, and demands the girl's name, but nothing will make Marius talk. Hugo lists the delights of that May: quarrelling over you and thou, discussing people they care nothing about, Cosette talking finery, Marius talking politics, listening knee to knee to carriages in the Rue de Babylone, keeping silence together.

Complications approach. One evening, as Marius comes along the Boulevard des Invalides with his head down, a voice says 'Good evening, Monsieur Marius.' It is Éponine. He has not thought of her once since the day she led him to the Rue Plumet, and though he owes her his happiness the meeting embarrasses him; absorbed in Cosette he has not even registered that this is Éponine Thénardier, bearer of the name in his father's will. He answers with 'you' rather than 'thou', and when she asks whether she has done anything to him, says no. She tries to speak, cannot smile, pauses twice with downcast eyes, then says good evening abruptly and goes.

title: A Cab Runs in English and Barks in Slang
summary: On the night of 3 June 1832 Éponine follows Marius to the Rue Plumet, finds the loosened bar, and sits guard beside it. Six men arrive to rob the house: Thénardier, out of prison, with Claquesous, Gueulemer, Babet, Brujon and Montparnasse. Éponine faces them down alone, threatening to scream and call the police, until Brujon reads bad omens in the day and the gang withdraws.
details: The next evening, 3 June, Marius sees Éponine coming through the trees of the boulevard and turns aside to reach the Rue Plumet by the Rue Monsieur. She follows him for the first time, sees him move the bar and slip in, finds the bar herself, mutters 'None of that, Lisette!' and sits on the stone footing of the railing in a dark nook where the gate meets the wall. A belated passer-by hears a threatening voice from the dark say she is no longer surprised he comes every evening, and hurries on.

Minutes later six men arrive separately along the wall and gather at the railing with putty for the window-pane, a drugged ball for the dog, and saws for the old bars. The sixth man, testing the bars, reaches the loose one, and a hand seizes his arm with the words 'There's a dog.' He recoils and asks what jade this is; she answers 'Your daughter.' It is Thénardier. The other five, Claquesous, Gueulemer, Babet, Brujon and Montparnasse, close in with their tools. Éponine throws herself on her father's neck, asks how he got out and how her mother is, and insists there is nothing to be had in the house: she was the one charged to investigate, and the people have moved. Babet points to a light moving in the attic, Toussaint spreading linen to dry. Hugo remarks that Éponine no longer speaks slang since she has known Marius.

When Thénardier pushes past to enter, she sets her back to the gate and tells the six armed men they shall not go in. If they touch the gate she will scream, beat on the door, rouse the street and call the police, beginning with her father. She laughs that she is the daughter of a wolf, that she will be hungry this summer and cold this winter, and that she does not care whether she is found dead on this pavement tomorrow or in the nets at Saint-Cloud a year hence; a dry cough racks her narrow chest. To her father's plea that they must eat she answers 'Burst!' and sits humming on the stone with her chin in her hand.

The six retreat under the lantern, humiliated. Babet guesses she is in love with the master of the house; Montparnasse offers to stay with her, knife open, while the others do the job; Thénardier says nothing. Brujon, the gang's oracle and the man who put up the job, says he saw two sparrows fighting that morning and jostled a quarrelling woman that evening, that it is all bad, and that they should quit. They go, agreeing to sleep 'under Pantin', Thénardier having the key to the gate. Éponine creeps after them to the boulevard and watches them melt into the dark.

title: Things of the Night
summary: A brief meditation: the Rue Plumet falls quiet again, and Hugo likens the ruffians' retreat before the girl to the way beasts of prey in a forest recoil from the spectral, the sinister stopping the merely ferocious.
details: After the ruffians leave, the street resumes its tranquil night aspect. Hugo observes that what has just happened would not have astonished a forest, where what is below man glimpses through the mists what is beyond man, and the forces of the gloom know and balance one another.

Teeth and claws, he says, fear what they cannot grasp; blood-drinking bestiality is uneasy before an impassive spectral form standing in its shroud. A black figure barring the way stops the wild beast short. That which comes from the cemetery intimidates that which comes from the cave: the ferocious fear the sinister, and wolves recoil when they meet a ghoul.

title: Marius Becomes Practical Once More to the Extent of Giving Cosette His Address
summary: That same evening Marius finds Cosette in tears: her father has told her to prepare for a journey, possibly to England, within the week. Marius, penniless and in debt, swears on his honour that he will die if she goes, tells her not to expect him the next evening because he is going to 'try something', and scratches his address, 16 Rue de la Verrerie, on the garden wall with his penknife.
details: While Éponine guards the gate, Marius is with Cosette under the most beautiful sky of that spring, and finds her weeping. Her father told her that morning to hold herself in readiness, to pack a large trunk for her and a small one for him, that he has business and must travel, that all is to be ready in a week and that they may go to England. Marius, who for six weeks has possessed Cosette as spirits possess, hears the words 'we are going away' as 'Cosette is not yours' and re-enters reality with a shock.

He asks coldly whether she will go; she answers 'If my father goes', and when he says he will then go elsewhere, she turns pale and understands him. She proposes that he follow wherever they go; he bursts out that he has no money, owes Courfeyrac more than ten louis, has a hat worth three francs and boots that let in water, and could not pay for a passport. He presses his brow against a tree for a long time while Cosette sobs beside him, then kneels and kisses the tip of her foot.

He gives her his word of honour, which he has never given anyone, feeling his father beside him: if she goes away, he will die. The solemnity of it stops her tears. He tells her not to expect him tomorrow but the day after, and mutters aside that 'he' is a man who never changes his habits and receives only in the evening, which Cosette does not understand. Saying she ought to know his address in case anything happens, he scratches '16 Rue de la Verrerie' into the plaster of the wall. Cosette promises to pray and to sing the music from Euryanthe he once listened to outside her shutters, and fixes nine o'clock the day after tomorrow. They kiss without noticing it, eyes on the stars. When Marius leaves, the street is empty: it is the moment Éponine is following the ruffians away. An idea he himself judges senseless has crossed his mind, and he has come to a desperate decision.

title: The Old Heart and the Young Heart in the Presence of Each Other
summary: Marius calls on his grandfather for the first time in four years to ask permission to marry Mademoiselle Fauchelevent. M. Gillenormand, who has been pining for him, meets him with harshness, softens at the word 'father', then wrecks everything by assuming the girl is a lancer's conquest and advising Marius to make her his mistress. Marius leaves with a farewell, and the old man collapses calling his name.
details: M. Gillenormand, past ninety-one, still lives with his daughter in the Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire, outwardly erect but inwardly sinking. For four years he has waited for Marius to ring his bell; now the idea that he may never see him again chills him. He keeps a portrait of his dead daughter, Madame Pontmercy, opposite his bed and remarks that it resembles 'him' too. When Mademoiselle Gillenormand ventures to ask whether he is still angry with poor Marius, he calls Marius a heartless ingrate and turns away to hide a tear, then forbids his name to be mentioned. Théodule, the lancer, has failed as a substitute: a vulgar chatterbox in a tricoloured cockade who only made the old man miss Marius more.

One evening, 24 June, as he sits before his fire thinking of Marius bitterly and lovingly, Basque announces 'M. Marius'. Marius enters, shabby, calm and sad. The grandfather, dazzled with joy, finds only harshness on his lips: 'What have you come here for?' Marius asks him to have pity on him; the old man retorts that youth is asking pity of a man of ninety-one who has lost his teeth and is losing his sight, and demands to know what he wants. Marius says he has come to ask permission to marry. Gillenormand summons his daughter to say good day and dismisses her, then interrogates him: no profession, nothing earned, only the twelve hundred livres allowance, a girl with no dowry and no expectations, a father he knows nothing of, named Mademoiselle Fauchelevent. He laughs and says 'Never, sir, never!'

Marius turns to go, and the single word 'Father' transforms the old man: he hauls Marius back into an armchair, tells him to jabber about his love affairs, gives him a hundred louis to buy a hat. Marius pours out the story: the Luxembourg, the garden with the iron fence in the Rue Plumet, the father who means to take her to England. At 'Rue Plumet' the grandfather drops his snuff: Théodule has told him of a girl behind a railing in the Rue Plumet near the barracks, a 'Pamela' the lancer has been courting. He treats the matter as an old man's gallantry, says one does not marry such a girl, and ends: 'Booby! make her your mistress.' The words enter Marius like a sword. He bows and says: 'Five years ago you insulted my father; today you have insulted my wife. I ask nothing more of you, sir. Farewell.' Gillenormand runs to the window shouting 'Marius!' four times, but he is already round the corner, and the old man falls back into his chair with nothing left in his eyes.

title: Jean Valjean
summary: The same day, Jean Valjean sits alone on the Champ-de-Mars, resolved to leave for England because he has seen Thénardier prowling the neighbourhood and the police are restless. That morning he found '16 Rue de la Verrerie' freshly scratched on the garden wall; now a folded paper drops on his knees reading 'Move away from your house', thrown by a figure in a grey blouse who vanishes over the parapet.
details: On 4 June, towards four in the afternoon, Jean Valjean sits in his workman's waistcoat and long-visored cap on a solitary slope of the Champ-de-Mars. He rarely goes out with Cosette now. For a week or two he has repeatedly caught sight of Thénardier on the boulevard, and though his own disguise saved him from recognition he is sure Thénardier is prowling nearby. Paris is unquiet, and police hunting political men like Pépin or Morey might easily stumble on a man like Jean Valjean. He has decided to leave Paris and France for England before the end of the week, and has warned Cosette.

An inexplicable thing has added to his alarm. That morning, alone in the garden before Cosette's shutters opened, he found a line freshly engraved on the wall, probably with a nail: '16 Rue de la Verrerie'. The grooves in the old black mortar were white and plaster dust powdered the nettles below. A signal to others, or a warning to him? In any case the garden has been violated. He recalls the earlier alarms of the household and says nothing to Cosette.

As he sits, a shadow tells him someone has stopped on the crest behind him, and a paper folded in four falls on his knees as if dropped over his head. In large pencilled letters it says: 'Move away from your house.' He springs up; no one is on the slope, but he sees a creature larger than a child and smaller than a man, in a grey blouse and dust-coloured velvet trousers, jump the parapet into the moat of the Champ-de-Mars. He goes home very thoughtful.

title: Marius
summary: Marius leaves his grandfather in despair, wanders the streets all night and day, pockets Javert's two loaded pistols, and vaguely hears fighting in Paris. At nine on 5 June he reaches the Rue Plumet: shutters closed, garden empty, no answer when he calls Cosette. Resolving to die, he hears a voice like Éponine's call through the trees that his friends await him at the barricade of the Rue de la Chanvrerie.
details: Marius has left M. Gillenormand with immense despair, though the grandfather's talk of Cousin Théodule has left no trace in his mind: at his age one suspects nothing, and he could sooner commit any crime than suspect Cosette. He wanders the streets till two in the morning, flings himself dressed on his mattress at Courfeyrac's, and wakes to find Courfeyrac, Enjolras, Feuilly and Combeferre standing hatted and ready to go out. 'Are you coming to General Lamarque's funeral?' Courfeyrac asks; it sounds like Chinese to him.

He goes out later and puts in his pocket the two pistols Javert gave him for the ambush of 3 February, still loaded, without knowing why. All day he prowls in intermittent rain, buys a penny roll and forgets it, apparently bathes in the Seine without noticing. He no longer hopes for anything; his one clear thought is that at nine he will see Cosette, and after that, gloom. From the deserted boulevards he hears strange noises and asks himself whether there is fighting.

At nine precisely he moves the bar and rushes into the garden. Cosette is not at her usual place nor in the recess by the steps; the shutters are closed; the garden is deserted. He knocks on the shutters, risking her father's face at the window, and calls 'Cosette!' twice. No reply. He sits on the steps, blesses his love, and tells himself that since Cosette is gone, all that remains is to die.

Then a voice from the street calls through the trees: 'Mr. Marius, are you there? Your friends are waiting for you at the barricade of the Rue de la Chanvrerie.' The voice is not wholly unfamiliar; it resembles the hoarse, rough voice of Éponine. He hurries to the gate, puts his head through, and sees someone who looks like a young man running off into the dark.

title: M. Mabeuf
summary: M. Mabeuf, who handed Jean Valjean's purse to the police as lost property, sinks into destitution: the plates and text of his Flora are gone, and he sells his rare books one by one for bread. When Mother Plutarque falls ill he sells his last treasure, the Diogenes Laertius, for a hundred francs on 4 June. The next afternoon, hearing that there is fighting near the Arsenal, he puts on his hat, reaches for a book that is no longer there, and walks out.
details: The purse Gavroche flung over the hedge did M. Mabeuf no good: unable to believe a star could coin itself into louis, he took it to the police commissioner as a lost article, and no one claimed it. Meanwhile his indigo experiments have failed at the Jardin des Plantes as in his garden, the pawnshop has sold the copper plates of his Flora to a coppersmith for stewpans, and he has sold the text as waste paper. He eats bread and potatoes, has sold his furniture, bedding, clothes, herbariums and prints, and keeps only his rarest books in a glass-fronted case: a Bible of 1560, a Tibullus printed by the Aldines, a unique Diogenes Laertius of 1644 among them. He burns no fire and goes to bed at sundown to save candles; people avoid him.

One day Mother Plutarque says she has no money for dinner and no one will give credit. Mabeuf looks over his books like a father choosing which child to sacrifice, goes out with one under his arm and comes back with thirty sous. From that day a veil falls over his face that never lifts. Day after day a book goes out and a coin comes back, dealers paying twenty sous for what cost him twenty francs. He says at times 'But I am eighty', as though hoping to reach the end of his days before the end of his books. Once he sells a Robert Estienne for thirty-five sous and buys an Aldus for forty, and goes without dinner, beaming. The Horticultural Society's president gets him invited to dine with the Minister; he sells an Elzevir for the cab fare, no one speaks to him all evening, the Minister's wife asks who that old gentleman is, and he walks home at midnight in a rainstorm.

His only pleasure is a few pages of the Diogenes Laertius each night. Then Mother Plutarque falls ill; the doctor orders an expensive potion and a nurse. The bookcase is empty except for that one volume. On 4 June 1832 he carries it to the Porte Saint-Jacques and returns with a hundred francs, which he lays in five-franc pieces on the old servant's nightstand without a word. Next morning he sits all morning on the overturned post in his garden, head drooping, in intermittent rain. In the afternoon shots and shouting break out over Paris. A passing gardener tells him it is the riots, that they are fighting near the Arsenal. Mabeuf takes his hat, mechanically feels for a book to put under his arm, finds none, says 'Ah! truly!' and goes off with a bewildered air.

title: The Surface of the Question
summary: Hugo opens the history of 5 June 1832 by asking what revolt is made of, and setting out the 'golden mean' school's case against uprisings: they cost France millions a day, depress trade, dishonour the July Revolution and end in massacres. He rejects this reasoning as looking only at effects, and promises to seek the cause.
details: Revolt, Hugo says, is composed of nothing and of everything: a wandering force that meets heads that speak, brains that dream, souls that suffer, and bears them away at random against the state, the laws and the insolence of others. Its elements range from embittered conviction and youthful courage to vanity, the taste for change and the rabble at the bottom, that mud which catches fire. Like a waterspout it carries off great natures and small, breaking one against the other, and gives whoever it seizes an extraordinary power, making a cannonball of a stone and a general of a porter. Some crafty politicians hold that a little revolt is hygienic for a government, since it tests the army and strengthens the police.

He then gives the floor to the school of the 'golden mean', the lukewarm-water party of demi-science. In its view the riots after 1830 spoiled the purity of the July Revolution, turning deliverance into catastrophe; every uprising closes shops, depresses the funds and shakes credit, at a cost reckoned at twenty million francs the first day, forty the second, sixty the third, the equivalent of a lost fleet. Uprisings have their beauty, this school concedes, the war of the pavements being as grand as the war of the thickets, lighting up Parisian generosity and bravery, but at the price of bloodshed, progress compromised, honest liberals in despair, foreign absolutism rejoicing, and the massacres of order grown ferocious over liberty gone mad. In sum: disastrous.

Thus speaks the bourgeoisie's approximation to wisdom. Hugo refuses the word 'uprisings' as too large and convenient, distinguishes one popular movement from another, and declines to weigh a revolt against a battle in francs: if July cost a hundred and twenty millions, the installation of Philip V in Spain cost two milliards, and he would still prefer the 14th of July. All the doctrinaire objection concerns effects; he will look for the cause, and promises to be explicit.

title: The Root of the Matter
summary: Hugo distinguishes insurrection, the war of the whole against a usurping fraction and therefore in the right, from revolt, the attack of the fraction against the whole, and runs through history sorting examples. He argues universal suffrage will one day make both obsolete, asks which June 1832 was, and announces that he will tell one little-known episode of 5 and 6 June, having seen it himself.
details: There is uprising and there is insurrection, two phases of wrath, one wrong and one right. In democratic states, when a fraction usurps, the whole may rise to reclaim its rights, even by arms: that is insurrection. The same cannon is wrong against the people on 10 August and right on 14 Vendémiaire. Machine-breaking, Ramus killed by students, Rousseau stoned in Switzerland, the salt smugglers who turned into Chouans, the Saint-Bartholomew assassins, the September cutthroats, the Vendée: these are revolt. Paris against the Bastille is insurrection. 'There is no insurrection except in a forward direction'; every violent step backward is a revolt against the human race. Danton against Louis XIV is insurrection; Hébert against Danton is revolt. Insurrection can be resurrection.

Before universal suffrage, each epoch protested as it could: under the Caesars there was no insurrection but there was Juvenal, and Tacitus, whose concentrated prose Hugo credits to the tyrant's compression of history, and whom God spared from meeting Caesar. Riot proceeds from a material fact, insurrection is a moral phenomenon; riot is Masaniello, insurrection Spartacus. A bread riot like Buzançais may start from a just grievance and still be a riot because it strikes blindly at the innocent. Every armed protest, even 14 July, begins as a torrent before becoming a river; some insurrections are lost in a swamp like the Rhine. Universal suffrage dissolves riot at birth by giving insurrection the vote, and whatever today may be, tomorrow will be peace. The bourgeois knows none of these shades: for him all is sedition, the dog biting its master, until the dog's head is suddenly outlined as a lion's and he shouts 'Long live the people!'

What then was the movement of June 1832, revolt or insurrection? Hugo will sometimes say revolt for the surface and keep insurrection for the foundation. Even those who call it an uprising speak of it with respect, as a relic of 1830, a last undulation of the mountain sinking into the plain. He closes by promising to relate facts the historian neglects, the foliage of great events, from the two days of 5 and 6 June, showing only one side and one episode, the least known, altering a few names, and able to say of what he tells: 'We have seen this.'

title: A Burial; An Occasion to Be Born Again
summary: The death of General Lamarque gives loaded Paris its spark. On 5 June 1832 his funeral procession crosses the city amid an armed and agitated crowd while the government holds fifty thousand troops ready. At the Austerlitz bridge, after Lafayette's farewell, a horseman with a red flag appears, dragoons meet the crowd, three shots are fired, and the riot explodes across the Faubourg Saint-Antoine.
details: In spring 1832, with the cholera three months old, Paris is long ripe for commotion; the spark is Lamarque's death. Lamarque had shown the bravery of the battlefield under the Empire and of the tribune under the Restoration, hated Wellington, kept the sadness of Waterloo for seventeen years, and died clasping a sword given him by the officers of the Hundred Days. His expected death was dreaded by the people as a loss and by the government as an occasion. On the eve and morning of 5 June the Faubourg Saint-Antoine arms itself: joiners take door-weights, a man sharpens a stocking-weaver's hook into a dagger, artisans are sent to Filspierre's for cartridges, drinkers in wineshops ask each other whether their pistols are under blouse or shirt, and leaders run from house to house.

On the 5th, a day of rain and sun, the procession crosses Paris with official pomp: two battalions with draped drums, ten thousand National Guards, the hearse drawn by young men, officers of the Invalides with laurel, then an innumerable crowd of students, refugees, strikers and printers under Spanish, Italian, German and Polish flags, brandishing sticks and sabres. Windows and roofs are full of anxious faces. The government has carabineers in the Place Louis XV, dragoons at the Célestins, artillery in the Louvre courtyard, twenty-four thousand soldiers in the city and thirty thousand outside. Rumours run through the cortège of Legitimist tricks, of the Duc de Reichstadt, of a factory of arms to be thrown open; among the noble emotions are also criminal faces saying 'Let us plunder!' Incidents mark the route: the coffin carried round the Vendôme column, stones at the Duc de Fitz-James on his balcony, an officer of the 12th Light declaring himself a Republican, the Polytechnic School arriving against orders. At the Bastille the Faubourg Saint-Antoine joins the throng and it begins to seethe; a man with a red beard is pointed out as the one who will give the word to fire.

At the esplanade of the Austerlitz bridge the hearse halts and Lafayette bids Lamarque farewell, all heads uncovered. Suddenly a man in black on horseback appears with a red flag, or a pike topped with a red cap; Lafayette turns away, Exelmans leaves the procession. Shouts go up of 'Lamarque to the Pantheon! Lafayette to the Town-hall!' and young men drag the hearse across the bridge and Lafayette's carriage along the Quai Morland. Dragoons emerge from the Célestins and advance at a walk; the crowd and the cavalry touch; no one knows what happened in that minute, a trumpet or a child's dagger-blow, but three shots are fired, killing the squadron chief Cholet and an old deaf woman closing her window. A woman screams 'They are beginning too soon!', a fresh squadron charges with bared swords, stones rain, a fusillade breaks out, the timber-yards of the Isle Louviers bristle with combatants and a barricade is begun. The cry 'To arms!' flies to all four quarters of Paris.

title: The Ebullitions of Former Days
summary: Within a quarter of an hour the riot breaks out at twenty points at once: armourers' shops are pillaged, flags appear, lanterns are smashed and barricades rise, twenty-seven in the Halles quarter alone. By five o'clock a third of Paris is in the insurgents' hands; the government under Soult, Lobau and Bugeaud hesitates as night falls and the Saint-Merry tocsin sounds, while Louis Philippe remains serene.
details: Nothing is more extraordinary than the first outbreak of a riot: foreseen but not prepared, coming from the pavements and from the clouds, plot here and improvisation there. Within fifteen minutes it is happening everywhere. Twenty bearded young men carry a crape-draped tricolour out of a dram-shop; a well-dressed bourgeois hands out cartridges in the street; a black flag reading 'Republic or Death!' is paraded in the Rue Saint-Pierre-Montmartre; section flags appear. A small-arms factory on the Boulevard Saint-Martin and three armourers' shops are stripped of two hundred and thirty guns, sixty-four swords and eighty-three pistols. Young men install themselves in women's houses to fire from the windows; a curiosity shop yields yataghans; a mason lies dead in the Rue de la Perle.

All over Paris men break lanterns, unharness carriages, tear up paving-stones and trees, roll out hogsheads and build barricades, forcing the bourgeois to help, requisitioning absent husbands' guns and chalking receipts on doors, disarming sentinels and tearing epaulets off officers. Students pour out of the Quartier Saint-Jacques and arms are distributed from the cafés. In one place only, the Rue Sainte-Avoye, the inhabitants tear down a barricade themselves; in one place only, the Rue du Temple, the insurgents abandon one. In less than an hour twenty-seven barricades spring up in the Halles quarter, centred on house No. 50, the fortress of Jeanne and his six hundred, with barricades at Saint-Merry and the Rue Maubuée, and countless others in the Marais, at Mont-Sainte-Geneviève, in the Rue Ménilmontant, and near the Prefecture of Police. Money is handed out at some barricades, passwords carried, sentinels posted; the tangled streets of the Halles are admirably chosen, and a dead man in the Rue du Ponceau carries a plan of Paris.

Within three hours the insurgents hold the Arsenal, the Marais, the Popincourt arms factory, the Château-d'Eau, the Veterans' barracks, Sainte-Pélagie, the Place Maubert and all the barriers; by five o'clock the Bastille, the Lingerie and the Blancs-Manteaux, with scouts menacing the Bank and the Post Office. A third of Paris is theirs, and the fighting has passed from stones to gunshots. At six the Passage du Saumon becomes a battlefield between the two fires, where the author of this book, gone to see the volcano close, sheltered half an hour behind a half-column. Drummers beating the call to arms are stabbed; three officers fall in the Rue Michel-le-Comte. The centre of Paris has become a colossal citadel where, tellingly, no fighting has yet begun. Some regiments waver, remembering the 53rd's neutrality in July 1830. Marshal Lobau and General Bugeaud command; huge patrols reconnoitre; the government, army in hand, hesitates as night comes and the Saint-Merry tocsin begins. Marshal Soult, who saw Austerlitz, looks on gloomily; reinforcements converge from Saint-Denis, Courbevoie and Vincennes, and around the Tuileries solitude forms. Louis Philippe is perfectly serene.

title: Originality of Paris
summary: Hugo describes the peculiar calm of Paris beyond the fighting quarters during an uprising, where shopkeepers remark on 'a squabble in the Rue Saint-Martin' and theatres play on; but this time, on 5 June 1832, the great city is afraid. Rumours fly, Soult hesitates, eight hundred are arrested by nine o'clock, and households listen behind bolted doors to the tocsin of Saint-Merry.
details: Ordinarily nothing is calmer than Paris outside the rebellious quarters. The shopkeeper hears the drum and says there seems to be a squabble in the Rue Saint-Martin or the Faubourg Saint-Antoine, 'or somewhere in that direction'; when platoon firing becomes audible he remarks that it is getting hot, shuts his shop and dons his uniform. Men fire in a square and grapeshot riddles house-fronts while a few streets away billiard-balls click in the cafés, theatres play vaudevilles and people go out to dinner. In 1831 a fusillade was stopped to let a wedding pass; in 1839 an old man wheeled a handcart of cocoa from barricade to troops and back, serving both sides. Only the size and gaiety of Paris, the city of Voltaire and Napoleon, make such a thing possible.

On this occasion, however, the city feels something stronger than itself: it is afraid. Doors and shutters close even in distant quarters; the courageous take arms and the cowards hide. Alarming news is hawked: that the insurgents hold the Bank, that six hundred are entrenched in the church of Saint-Merry, that the line cannot be relied on, that Marshal Clausel told Armand Carrel to get a regiment first, that Lafayette, though ill, said he would follow wherever there was room for a chair, that pillagers would roam the deserted corners at night, that Lobau and Bugeaud would march four columns on the centre at midnight or dawn, or that the troops might evacuate Paris altogether. People wonder why Soult does not attack; the old lion seems to scent an unknown monster in the gloom.

Evening comes; the theatres do not open; patrols search passers-by and arrest suspects, more than eight hundred by nine o'clock, filling the Prefecture, the Conciergerie and La Force. In the Conciergerie's long vault prisoners lie heaped on straw, harangued by Lagrange of Lyons. People barricade themselves at home, wives and mothers ask why he has not come home, and everyone listens on the threshold to cavalry, caissons, trumpets, firing, and above all to the lamentable alarm peal of Saint-Merry, waiting for the first cannon-shot and asking how it will all end.

title: Some Explanations with Regard to the Origin of Gavroche’s Poetry
summary: As the funeral crowd scatters in panic, Gavroche borrows an old holster-pistol from a bric-a-brac shop and marches off to the wars singing, discovering on the boulevard that it has no trigger. Hugo explains his songs and tells how the two little boys he sheltered in the elephant, his own brothers unknown to him, never came back to the meeting-place.
details: When the clash at the Arsenal sends a frightful ebb back through the crowd on the boulevards, a ragged child coming down the Rue Ménilmontant with a sprig of laburnum spots an old holster-pistol in a bric-a-brac window, tells the shopwoman he is borrowing her machine, and runs off with it. Fleeing bourgeois in the Rue Amelot meet him brandishing it and singing a couplet about pointed hats. It is little Gavroche on his way to the wars. On the boulevard he notices the pistol has no trigger.

Hugo wonders who wrote the songs Gavroche sings; perhaps Gavroche himself. He knows every popular tune and mixes in his own chirpings, the repertory of the birds with the repertory of the workshops; he knows thieves, was apprenticed three months to a printer, and once ran an errand for an Academician: a gamin of letters. He has no idea that the two brats he housed in his elephant that rainy night were his own brothers. Having spent that night with his brothers and the dawn with his father, he fetched the two from the elephant at daybreak, shared some invented breakfast, entrusted them to the street, and told them to come back in the evening if they did not find papa and mamma. They never returned, picked up by a policeman, stolen by a mountebank, or simply lost in the Chinese puzzle of Paris; ten or twelve weeks later he still scratches his head and asks where the devil his two children are.

In the Rue du Pont-aux-Choux the only shop open is a pastrycook's; he searches his pockets, finds not a sou, and shouts 'Help!' at missing the last cake. Passing through the Rue du Parc-Royal he consoles himself by tearing down theatre posters in broad daylight, and spits philosophical bile at a group of fat, comfortable proprietors who, he says, eat their money.

title: Gavroche on the March
summary: Gavroche parades his triggerless pistol through the Marais, pausing to help a fallen lancer and his horse, then interrupts four old gossips in the Rue de Thorigny and is howled at as a beggar's brat and a bastard. He pities a starving poodle and heads for the Orme-Saint-Gervais.
details: Waving his pistol in the open street, Gavroche feels his fervour grow. Between scraps of the Marseillaise he harangues the bourgeois, declares the police spies dogs, announces that the boulevard is coming to the boil and that he gives his days to his country and will never see his concubine Nini again. When a National Guard lancer's horse falls he lays down the pistol, helps the man up and the horse too, then resumes his march. The Rue de Thorigny is all peace and silence, in the Marais's usual apathy.

Four old women gossip in a doorway, three portresses and a ragpicker with her basket, standing at the four corners of old age. The ragpicker, humble and grateful in the hierarchy of refuse heaps, listens as they talk of cats and dogs, the King of Rome's sheep-carriage, the Duc de Bordeaux, Louis XVIII, and the dreadful price of meat; then boasts of how she sorts her haul at home, rags in a basket, bones under the bed. Gavroche, listening behind her, asks what they mean by talking politics, and is met with a quadruple howl: another rascal, with a pistol in his paddle, the sort who is never easy unless overturning the authorities. He thumbs his nose.

Mother Patagon the portress foresees evil doings, says the errand-boy next door now carries a gun instead of a girl in a pink bonnet, that there was a revolution at Pontoise, that the Célestins are full of pistols, that tobacco will get dearer, and that she will go to see him guillotined. Gavroche tells her to blow her promontory and passes on, reflecting in the Rue Pavée that the ragpicker is wrong to insult revolutionists since his pistol is in her interest. Patagon follows to shout 'You're nothing but a bastard' after him; he does not care a brass farthing. Passing the Hotel Lamoignon he cries 'Forward march to the battle!', reproaches his pistol that he is going off but it will not, pities a gaunt poodle whose hoops all show, and turns towards the Orme-Saint-Gervais.

title: Just Indignation of a Hairdresser
summary: The hairdresser who turned Gavroche's two little protégés out of his shop is shaving an old soldier of the Empire and discussing the Emperor's horse and wounds when a stone smashes his window. It is Gavroche, who has not forgotten the two brats, saying good day on his way past.
details: The barber near the Orme-Saint-Gervais is shaving a veteran of the legion who served under the Empire. From the riot and Lamarque they pass to the Emperor: how he rode (badly, but he never fell because he did not know how to fall), his white racing mare with a black star, his one wound, in the heel at Ratisbon. The veteran lists his own wounds, two sabre-blows at Marengo, a bullet at Austerlitz, another at Jena, a bayonet at Friedland, seven or eight lance-thrusts at the Moskowa, a shell splinter at Lutzen, a biscaïen ball in the thigh at Waterloo, 'that's all'. The hairdresser declares grandly that he would rather die of a cannonball in the belly than slowly in bed with drugs and syringes; the soldier remarks that he is not over fastidious.

A fearful crash shatters the show-window. The wig-maker turns pale and cries that it is a cannonball. The soldier picks up what is rolling on the floor: a pebble. At the broken window the hairdresser sees Gavroche fleeing at full speed towards the Marché Saint-Jean. Passing the shop with the two brats still in his mind, Gavroche had been unable to resist saying good day with a stone. The hairdresser, from white turned blue, shrieks that the fellow does mischief for the pure pleasure of it: 'What has anyone done to that gamin?'

title: The Child Is Amazed at the Old Man
summary: At the Marché Saint-Jean Gavroche joins the armed band led by Enjolras, Courfeyrac, Combeferre and Feuilly, swelled by Bahorel and Jean Prouvaire. Bahorel in his scarlet waistcoat tears down an archbishop's Lenten notice and wins Gavroche's admiration, and Enjolras rebukes him for wasting his wrath. Marching among them, unarmed and hurrying, is a very old man: M. Mabeuf.
details: In the Marché Saint-Jean, where the post has already been disarmed, Gavroche 'effects a junction' with a band led by Enjolras with a double-barrelled hunting-gun, Combeferre with a National Guard's musket and two pistols, Jean Prouvaire with an old cavalry musket, Bahorel with a rifle, Courfeyrac brandishing a sword-cane, and Feuilly at their head with a naked sword shouting 'Long live Poland!' Cravatless, hatless, soaked, with lightning in their eyes, they reach the Quai Morland; Gavroche asks where they are going and Courfeyrac tells him to come along.

Bahorel, like a fish in water in a riot, wears a scarlet waistcoat that makes a passer-by cry 'Here are the reds!'; he retorts that he does not tremble before a poppy and leaves fear of red to horned cattle. Spotting the Archbishop of Paris's Lenten permission to eat eggs addressed to his 'flock', he calls flock a polite word for geese and tears it down, which conquers Gavroche. Enjolras tells him he is wrong: the Archbishop is not the enemy, and one does not fire out of the ranks with the soul any more than with a gun. Bahorel answers that each has his own fashion, that he wants to eat eggs without permission, and that he is only whetting his appetite, 'Hercle!' Gavroche asks what Hercle means and is told it is Latin for cursed name of a dog; when Bahorel shouts 'para bellum' for cartridges to a bearded young man at a window, Gavroche, now understanding Latin, approves.

A tumultuous retinue of students, artists, members of the Cougourde of Aix, artisans and longshoremen follows with clubs and bayonets. Among them walks an extremely old man, unarmed, hurrying so as not to be left behind, with a thoughtful air. Gavroche asks Courfeyrac 'Keksekça?' and is told he is an old duffer. It is M. Mabeuf.

title: The Old Man
summary: Hugo explains how Mabeuf came to be in the band: Courfeyrac met him zigzagging hatless in the rain near the dragoon charge, told him there would be fighting and that they were going to fling the government to the earth, and the old man answered 'That is good' and followed. The students take him for an old regicide of the Convention. Gavroche leads the way singing towards Saint-Merry.
details: Enjolras and his friends were on the Boulevard Bourdon when the dragoons charged, and fled into the Rue Bassompierre shouting 'To the barricades!' In the Rue Lesdiguières they met an old man walking in a zigzag as if drunk, hat in hand though it was raining hard. Courfeyrac recognised Father Mabeuf, whom he knew from having often walked Marius to his door, and, amazed to see the timid old beadle-book-collector strolling among bullets, told him to go home. 'Why?' 'There's going to be a row.' 'That's well.' Sword-thrusts and firing, cannon: 'That is good.' Where are you going? 'We are going to fling the government to the earth.' 'That is good.'

He has followed them ever since without a word, his step suddenly firm, refusing the arms artisans offer him, marching near the front rank with the gait of a man walking and the face of a man asleep. The students mutter what a fierce old fellow he is, and the rumour spreads that he is a former member of the Convention, an old regicide. The mob turns through the Rue de la Verrerie.

Little Gavroche marches ahead like a trumpet, singing a nonsense ballad of Charlot and Charlotte and two drunken sparrows, with refrains for Chatou, Passy, Meudon and Pantin. They head for Saint-Merry.

title: Recruits
summary: Near the Rue des Billettes a tall grey-haired stranger of bold bearing joins the band unnoticed by Gavroche. Passing his own door in the Rue de la Verrerie, Courfeyrac runs up for his hat, his purse and a large hidden coffer, and finds a pale, slight young workman who has waited an hour asking for Marius; told Courfeyrac is going to the barricades, the youth asks to come. The mob overshoots Saint-Merry and ends up in the Rue Saint-Denis.
details: The band grows every moment. Near the Rue des Billettes a man of lofty stature with greying hair and a bold, daring mien joins them; Courfeyrac, Enjolras and Combeferre notice him but none of them knows him. Gavroche, busy singing, whistling and pounding shutters with the butt of his triggerless pistol, pays him no attention.

In the Rue de la Verrerie they pass Courfeyrac's door. Saying he has forgotten his purse and lost his hat, he runs upstairs and seizes an old hat, his purse, and a large square coffer the size of a valise hidden under his soiled linen. Coming down, the portress hails him as 'Monsieur de Courfeyrac', which he threatens to repay by calling her Mother de Veuvain, and tells him someone has been waiting over an hour in her lodge. Out comes a pale, thin, small, freckled artisan in a tattered blouse and patched velvet trousers, with rather the air of a girl dressed as a man but a voice not at all like a woman's, who asks for Monsieur Marius.

Courfeyrac says Marius is not there, that he does not know whether he will return, and that he himself will not come back because he is going to the barricades. The youth asks why, where, offers to carry the coffer, and asks to come along; Courfeyrac says the street is free and the pavements belong to everyone, and runs to rejoin his friends, giving the coffer to one of them. A quarter of an hour later he notices the young man has actually followed. A mob does not go precisely where it intends: they overshoot Saint-Merry and find themselves, without quite knowing how, in the Rue Saint-Denis.

title: History of Corinthe from Its Foundation
summary: Hugo maps the tangle of streets by the Halles where the Rue de la Chanvrerie lay, and tells the history of the wine-shop Corinthe: the Pot-aux-Roses renamed for a painted bunch of Corinth grapes, Father Hucheloup's stuffed carps and his sign that rain turned into 'Carpe ho ras', his death in 1830, his bearded widow, the two serving-maids Matelote and Gibelotte, and the shabby upstairs room where Courfeyrac's friends ate and drank on credit.
details: Parisians who today see a basket-maker's sign of Napoleon in willow opposite the Rue Mondétour have no idea what happened there thirty years ago. That is where the Rue de la Chanvrerie and the wine-shop Corinthe stood, site of a barricade eclipsed by Saint-Merry's, on which Hugo means to shed light. As with Waterloo, he gives a letter: imagine an N with its top on the Rue Saint-Denis and its base on the Halles, the uprights the Rue de la Grande-Truanderie and the Rue de la Chanvrerie, the crossbar the Rue de la Petite-Truanderie, with the Rue Mondétour cutting all three at crooked angles: seven islands of eight-storey houses shored up with beams, wet pavements, cellar-like stalls and century-old gratings, all since devoured by the Rue Rambuteau. Entering the Rue de la Chanvrerie from the Rue Saint-Denis one found it narrowing like a funnel into what looked like a blind alley, with two dark cuts of the Rue Mondétour left and right, and at the bottom a two-storey house forming a cape in the street.

There a wine-shop had stood three hundred years, on the spot old Theophilus wrote of a poor lover's skeleton swinging. In Régnier's day it was the Pot-aux-Roses, with a rose-painted post for a rebus sign; in the last century the painter Natoire, grateful for his drinking bouts there, painted a bunch of Corinth grapes on the post, the landlord added 'Au Raisin de Corinthe', and the ellipsis of drunkards made it Corinthe. The last of the dynasty, Father Hucheloup, painted the post blue. Taproom and kitchen below, billiard-room above reached by a spiral stair, the family's lodging on the second floor up a ladder, servants in the mansards, a trapdoor to the cellar. Hucheloup, cook rather than chemist, invented stuffed carps, carpes au gras, and advertised them on his wall in his own spelling, 'Carpes ho gras'; rain washed out an S and a G, leaving 'Carpe ho ras', so that knowing no French he had equalled Horace, and the advice also meant 'Enter my wine-shop'. All of it vanished when the Mondétour labyrinth was opened up in 1847.

Corinthe was the meeting-place of Courfeyrac and his friends; Grantaire discovered it, entering for the Carpe horas and returning for the carpes au gras. They ate, drank, shouted, paid badly or not at all, and were always welcome. Hucheloup, a moustached former fencing-master, growled at customers and then burst out laughing, a snuffbox shaped like a pistol. He died about 1830, taking the secret of the carps with him; his inconsolable widow, bearded and homely, kept on, the cooking became execrable and the bad wine worse, and the friends kept coming 'out of pity', as Bossuet said. Mother Hucheloup, breathless and misshapen, mangled her rustic reminiscences with her pronunciation. The first-floor room, lit by one narrow window and a lamp always burning, had three-legged furniture and a charcoal quatrain on the wall mocking the wart on her nose, before which she passed all day untroubled. Two maids, Matelote, large, plump, red-haired and noisy, the late Hucheloup's favourite, and Gibelotte, tall, pale, languid, first up and last to bed, waiting silently on everyone with a sleepy smile, served the poor wine and broth. On the door Courfeyrac had chalked: 'Régale si tu peux et mange si tu l'oses.'

title: Preliminary Gayeties
summary: On the morning of 5 June Laigle (Bossuet) and Joly breakfast at Corinthe and are joined by Grantaire, who drinks and harangues against God's bankrupt universe. A small gamin named Navet brings Bossuet the password 'A.B.C.' from Enjolras, but the three decide to stay and drink; by two they are deep in bottles when Bossuet, at the window, sees Enjolras, Gavroche and the armed band pass the end of the street, and shouts to Courfeyrac that this is a good place to build his barricade.
details: Laigle de Meaux lives with Joly as a bird lives on a branch, the two sharing everything, even Musichetta to some extent. At nine on the morning of 5 June, Joly stuffed up with a cold, they climb to Corinthe's first floor and order oysters, cheese and ham from Matelote and Gibelotte. Grantaire's head appears at the hatchway, drawn, he says, by the smell of Brie; Gibelotte sets two bottles before him. He drinks while the others eat, teases Laigle about his old coat, and when Laigle marvels at how quiet the street is with Paris turned upside down and recalls the convents that once swarmed there, Grantaire launches a long harangue: a bad oyster has brought back his hypochondria; a pretty grisette he knows has just become a banker's mistress and looks no worse for it; right is Brennus taking Rome and crying 'Vae victis'; there is but one reality, drink. As for revolution, it proves only that God is in a quandary, patching events like a tradesman with an empty till giving a ball; creation is bankrupt; he should have been born a Turk. It is folly to massacre each other in June when they might be out in the hay.

Joly remarks that it is aberrant that Marius is in love, and Grantaire imagines the pair, souls who forget to kiss and lie among the stars. A ragged boy under ten climbs in and asks for Monsieur Bossuet: a tall blonde fellow on the boulevard paid him ten sous to say 'A.B.C.' Laigle borrows ten sous from each friend and gives the child twenty; he gives his name as Navet, Gavroche's friend, declines breakfast because he must shout 'Down with Polignac!' in the procession, and scrapes a bow. Laigle decodes A.B.C. as the burial of Lamarque and Grantaire names the blonde as Enjolras sending a warning. Joly will not go through water, Grantaire prefers a breakfast to a hearse, and Laigle concludes they stay: they may miss the funeral without missing the riot. Grantaire mutters that Enjolras disdains him and sent to Bossuet, not to him.

By two in the afternoon the table is covered with empty bottles and two candles burn in the gloom of the storm-dark room. Grantaire has passed from wine to the beer-glass, the abyss, mixing brandy, stout and absinthe; still gay, he proclaims that everyone shall be an Academician with the right to embrace Madame Hucheloup, and asks who has unhooked the stars to put them on the table as candles. Joly tells the maids to give him no more; he has drunk two francs ninety-five since morning. Bossuet, very drunk but composed, sits on the sill of the open window with his back in the rain and hears a tumult: in the Rue Saint-Denis at the end of the street pass Enjolras with his gun, Gavroche with his pistol, Feuilly and Courfeyrac with swords, Jean Prouvaire, Combeferre, Bahorel and the whole armed rabble. He makes a trumpet of his hands and bellows for Courfeyrac, who comes a few paces up the street and says they are going to make a barricade. 'Well, here! This is a good place! Make it here!' Courfeyrac agrees, and at his signal the mob pours into the Rue de la Chanvrerie.

title: Night Begins to Descend Upon Grantaire
summary: The mob builds a barricade across the Rue de la Chanvrerie in minutes from torn-out bars, paving-stones, a lime-dealer's dray, Mother Hucheloup's casks and an omnibus that Bossuet stops and overturns. Grantaire, roaring drunk, declaims about Matelote until Enjolras orders him off the barricade; abruptly sobered, he begs to be left to sleep there 'until I die', is told he is incapable of believing or dying, answers 'You will see', and falls asleep at a table.
details: The spot is admirably suited: the street widens at its mouth and narrows into a pocket, Corinthe blocks the end, the Rue Mondétour is easily barricaded on either side, and attack is possible only from the Rue Saint-Denis, in front and in full view. Terror seizes the street; every shutter slams from ground floor to roof, and an old woman hangs a mattress before her window against musketry. Only the wine-shop stays open, because the mob has rushed into it; Mame Hucheloup sighs 'Ah my God!' Joly leans out to tell Courfeyrac he should have brought an umbrella.

In minutes twenty iron bars are wrenched from the wine-shop's grating and ten fathoms of street unpaved; Gavroche and Bahorel seize and overturn the dray of a lime-dealer named Anceau with its three barrels of lime; Enjolras raises the cellar trap and the widow's empty casks flank the lime; Feuilly, whose fingers paint fan-sticks, backs it all with heaps of rough stone, and beams torn from house-fronts are laid on the casks. Half the street is barred higher than a man before Bossuet and Courfeyrac turn round. Matelote and Gibelotte carry rubbish, Gibelotte serving the barricade as sleepily as she serves wine. An omnibus with two white horses passes the end of the street; Bossuet runs out, makes the passengers alight, hands down 'the ladies', dismisses the conductor and leads it back by the bridle, declaring in Latin that not everyone may go to Corinth. Unharnessed, the horses wander off down the Rue Mondétour, and the omnibus on its side completes the bar.

Mame Hucheloup takes refuge upstairs muttering that the end of the world has come; Joly kisses her fat red neck and tells Grantaire a woman's neck is an infinitely delicate thing. Grantaire, at the height of dithyramb, seizes Matelote round the waist and proclaims from the window that she is a chimaera born of a Gothic Pygmalion's love for a gargoyle, that she and the moustached Mother Hucheloup will fight like hussars and terrify the suburbs, that he understands only love and liberty, and that if kind hearts had fat purses there would be no more poor: he pictures Jesus Christ with Rothschild's fortune. Courfeyrac tells him to hold his tongue, 'you cask'. Enjolras, standing on the crest of the barricade gun in hand, raises his austere face and shouts at Grantaire to go and sleep off his wine elsewhere: this is the place for enthusiasm, not drunkenness, and he must not disgrace the barricade.

The rebuke works like cold water in the face. Suddenly sober, Grantaire sits at a table by the window, looks at Enjolras with indescribable gentleness and says 'Let me sleep here.' Enjolras tells him to sleep elsewhere. Grantaire, his tender troubled eyes still on him: 'Let me sleep here—until I die.' Enjolras, disdainful: 'Grantaire, you are incapable of believing, of thinking, of willing, of living, and of dying.' Grantaire gravely answers 'You will see', stammers a few words, drops his head on the table and is asleep within the instant.

title: An Attempt to Console the Widow Hucheloup
summary: Courfeyrac tells the widow Hucheloup that her table is being used to avenge the hundred-franc fine she once paid, and Hugo describes the fifty motley defenders building two barricades at right angles around Corinthe, casting bullets from her pewter while the women make lint. The tall stranger from the Rue des Billettes works on the small barricade, the young workman who asked for Marius has vanished, and Gavroche, a whirlwind everywhere at once, demands a real gun and is told the men come first.
details: Bahorel exults that the street looks well in its low-necked dress. Courfeyrac, demolishing the wine-shop, reminds Mother Hucheloup of the hundred-franc fine she paid when Gibelotte shook a counterpane out of the window and a flowerpot fell into the street, and tells her they are avenging her, a consolation she finds as useful as the Arab father who, asked to avenge a slap on his daughter's left cheek, slapped her right one and sent her to tell her husband the score was even. The rain stops. Recruits bring a barrel of powder under their blouses, bottles of vitriol, carnival torches and fire-pots left over from the King's festival of 1 May, said to come from a grocer named Pépin in the Faubourg Saint-Antoine; they smash every street-lantern in the Rue de la Chanvrerie and the streets around.

Enjolras, Combeferre and Courfeyrac direct everything. Two barricades rise at right angles resting on the Corinthe house, the large one across the Rue de la Chanvrerie, a narrow one of casks and paving-stones across the Rue Mondétour towards the Rue du Cygne. About fifty men work, thirty of them armed from a wholesale loan on an armourer's shop: one in a round-jacket with a cavalry sabre and holster-pistols, one in shirtsleeves with a powder-horn, one in a breastplate of nine sheets of grey paper armed with a saddler's awl, one vowing to die at the point of a bayonet he does not possess, one wearing a National Guard's cartridge-box lettered 'Public Order'. All ages and faces, pale young men and bronzed longshoremen, brothers who do not know each other's names, discuss their chances: succour at three in the morning, a regiment that is sure, Paris rising. In the kitchen they melt the establishment's pewter mugs, spoons and forks into bullets; in the billiard-room Mame Hucheloup, Matelote and Gibelotte, variously stupefied, breathless and roused by terror, tear dishcloths into lint with three bushy-bearded insurgents.

The tall man noticed at the Rue des Billettes is at work on the smaller barricade, making himself useful. Gavroche works on the larger one. The young man who had waited for Courfeyrac and asked for Marius disappeared about the time the omnibus was overturned. Gavroche is a whirlwind, climbing, whistling, pricking a student here and biting an artisan there, a fly on the revolutionary coach, shouting for more paving-stones and casks and insisting that a glass door is excellent in a barricade because it cuts the corns of the National Guard. Furious at his triggerless pistol, he goes from man to man demanding a gun; he had one in 1830, he says, when they had a dispute with Charles X. Enjolras shrugs: when there are enough for the men they will give some to the children. Gavroche answers haughtily that if Enjolras is killed before him he will take his, and the two exchange 'Gamin!' and 'Greenhorn!' A lost dandy at the end of the street flees when Gavroche invites him to do something for his country.

title: Preparations
summary: Hugo describes the finished redoubt: a main barricade six or seven feet high with interior steps and an exit gap, a red flag on the upright omnibus pole, the hidden Mondétour barricade, and a passage left open towards the Rue des Prêcheurs. Courfeyrac opens the coffer and hands each man thirty cartridges, Enjolras posts three sentinels, and the fifty wait in the deepening twilight, armed and tranquil.
details: The newspapers that called the Rue de la Chanvrerie barricade a nearly impregnable structure reaching the first floor were wrong: it averaged six or seven feet, built so that defenders could hide behind it or mount its crest by a quadruple row of paving-stone steps inside. Outside, paving-stones and casks bound with beams and planks tangled in the wheels of Anceau's dray and the overturned omnibus gave it a bristling look. A gap wide enough for a man was left between the houses and the end furthest from the wine-shop; the omnibus pole stood upright roped in place, a red flag floating from it. The little Mondétour barricade, hidden behind the wine-shop, made the whole a redoubt. Enjolras and Courfeyrac deliberately left the other fragment of the Rue Mondétour, opening through the Rue des Prêcheurs into the Halles, unbarricaded, to keep a line to the outside, fearing no attack from that difficult street. Inside, an irregular square with twenty paces between the barrier and the tall, inhabited but tightly shut houses at the back.

All this is done in under an hour without a single bearskin or bayonet appearing; bourgeois who still venture into the Rue Saint-Denis glance down the street and hurry on. With the barricades finished and the flag up, a table is dragged out, Courfeyrac mounts it, Enjolras brings the square coffer and Courfeyrac opens it: cartridges. A tremor and a silence pass through the bravest. Courfeyrac distributes them with a smile, thirty to each man; many have powder and make more with the bullets they have cast. The barrel of powder is set on a table by the door in reserve.

The alarm beating through Paris has become a monotonous noise they no longer heed, receding and returning in melancholy undulations. They load guns and carbines together, without haste, with solemn gravity. Enjolras posts three sentinels outside: in the Rue de la Chanvrerie, in the Rue des Prêcheurs, and at the corner of the Rue de la Petite-Truanderie. Then they wait, alone in streets no one passes any more, among dumb houses that seem dead, as the twilight deepens and something can be felt advancing through the silence.

title: Waiting
summary: While bullets are cast and lint made, Combeferre, Courfeyrac, Feuilly, Bossuet, Joly, Bahorel and others gather in a corner of the wine-shop as in their student days, and Jean Prouvaire murmurs in the dusk a long poem recalling a young love in a Latin Quarter garret. A torch set in a cage of paving-stones lights the red flag and nothing else.
details: Hugo asks what they did during those hours of waiting, and answers that he must tell, since it is history. While men mould bullets over a brazier and women make lint, while sentinels watch and Enjolras keeps an eye on the sentinels, Combeferre, Courfeyrac, Jean Prouvaire, Feuilly, Bossuet, Joly, Bahorel and some others seek each other out and sit together in a corner of the wine-shop turned casemate, loaded carbines leaning on their chairs, as in the most peaceful days of their student conversations, and begin to recite love verses.

The poem, murmured in a low voice in the dusk by Jean Prouvaire, the gentle poet, asks a woman whether she remembers their sweet life when they were both so young that their ages together did not make forty, when he was a briefless lawyer taking her to dine at the Prado and the roses seemed to turn to look at her; the garret in the Latin Quarter where the Sorbonne was their pastoral spot, the Place Maubert and the Place Dauphine, a flower she gave him that proved celestial goodness better than Malebranche or Lamennais, her burnt muff and lost boa, the portrait of Shakespeare sold one evening for supper, a Dante in folio for a table to eat a hundred chestnuts, the first kiss that left him pale and believing in God, and all the sighs from hearts full of shadow flown into the deep heavens. The hour, the place, the stars beginning to show, the funereal calm of the deserted streets and the imminence of the inexorable adventure give the verses a pathetic charm.

Meanwhile a lamp is lit in the small barricade, and in the large one a wax torch of the kind seen on Shrove Tuesday before carts of masks bound for la Courtille, brought from the Faubourg Saint-Antoine. It is set in a cage of paving-stones closed on three sides against the wind and arranged so that all its light falls on the flag; street and barricade stay sunk in gloom, and nothing is visible but the red flag, lit as if by an enormous dark-lantern, its scarlet deepened to a terrible purple.

title: The Man Recruited in the Rue des Billettes
summary: Night falls and nothing comes. Enjolras sends Gavroche out to scout, but the gamin first points out the tall stranger from the Rue des Billettes as a police spy who pulled him off a cornice by the ear two weeks ago. Challenged, the man declares himself an agent of the authorities named Javert; he is seized, searched, found to carry an inspector's card and a note from the Prefect, bound to the post in the taproom, and told he will be shot ten minutes before the barricade is taken. Gavroche leaves with Javert's gun.
details: Night is fully come and only distant, scattered fusillades are heard; the government is taking its time. Fifty men are waiting for sixty thousand. Enjolras, impatient, goes to find Gavroche, who is making cartridges in the taproom by two candles on the counter. Gavroche is preoccupied, but not with his cartridges: the man of the Rue des Billettes has just come in with the large musket that fell to his share and sat down at the least lighted table, and the gamin, following him with his eyes, has sprung to his feet. The man had been observing everything in the barricade with singular attention until he entered this room, where he has fallen into a brown study. Gavroche circles him on tiptoe, his face running through every grimace of disbelief, uncertainty and conviction; a great event has plainly happened in his life.

Enjolras tells him he is small and will not be seen: slip out, skirt the houses, skirmish about the streets and come back to report. Gavroche agrees, says the little chaps are good for something, then lowers his voice and nods at the tall man: 'He's a police spy.' Asked whether he is sure, he says it is not two weeks since the man pulled him off the cornice of the Pont Royal by the ear. Enjolras whispers to a longshoreman, who returns with three more broad-shouldered porters; they take their places behind the stranger's table. Enjolras asks him who he is. The man plunges his gaze into Enjolras's clear eyes, smiles with disdainful resolution and says 'I see what it is. Well, yes!' 'You are a police spy?' 'I am an agent of the authorities.' 'And your name?' 'Javert.'

At a sign the four porters collar him, throw him down, pinion and search him before he can turn round. They find a small round card between two pieces of glass bearing the arms of France, the motto 'Supervision and vigilance', the note 'Javert, inspector of police, aged fifty-two' and the signature of the Prefect Gisquet, plus his watch and purse of gold, which they leave him, and under the watch an envelope in the Prefect's own hand ordering Inspector Javert, once his political mission is done, to verify by special supervision whether malefactors have intrigues on the right bank near the Jena bridge. They bind his arms behind him and tie him to the famous post in the middle of the room that once gave the wine-shop its name. Gavroche steps up: 'It's the mouse who has caught the cat.' Javert has not uttered a cry.

Courfeyrac, Bossuet, Joly, Combeferre and the men from both barricades come running at the sight. Javert, roped to the post, raises his head with the serenity of a man who has never lied. Enjolras tells him he will be shot ten minutes before the barricade is taken. 'Why not at once?' 'We are saving our powder.' 'Then finish the business with a blow from a knife.' 'Spy, we are judges and not assassins.' Enjolras sends Gavroche about his errand; the gamin asks for the spy's gun as he goes, saying he leaves them the musician but wants the clarinet, gives a military salute, and passes out through the gap in the large barricade.

title: Many Interrogation Points with Regard to a Certain le Cabuc
summary: A drunken stranger called Le Cabuc tries to break into the tall house at the end of the barricade to fire from its windows, and when the old porter refuses to open, shoots him dead at his window. Enjolras forces him to his knees, gives him a minute to pray, and executes him with a pistol to the ear, then tells the barricade that insurrection must have its discipline and that he has judged himself too. Hugo adds that a police card was later found on the body and that police tradition says Le Cabuc was Claquesous. The young man who asked for Marius reappears on the barricade.
details: Hugo will not omit an incident of epic and savage horror that occurred just after Gavroche left. Among the passers-by who joined the mob was a man in a threadbare porter's jacket, drunk or feigning it, called Le Cabuc, a stranger even to those who claimed to know him. Drinking at a table dragged outside the wine-shop, he eyes the five-storey house at the end of the barricade commanding the street towards the Rue Saint-Denis and declares they must fire from there. The door is shut; he knocks three times with the massive knocker, shouts, then batters it with a gun-butt, but it is an old oak alley door lined with iron, a prison postern. At last a small window opens on the third floor and a grey-haired old porter with a candle asks what the gentlemen want. 'Open!' 'That cannot be, gentlemen.' Le Cabuc levels his gun in the dark; the porter, who cannot see him, says no again, and the shot takes him under the chin and out at the nape. The candle falls, and a motionless head lies on the sill with a little white smoke drifting up.

'There!' says Le Cabuc, grounding his gun; and a hand like an eagle's talon falls on his shoulder with the words 'On your knees.' It is Enjolras, pistol in hand, pale, bare-necked, with his woman's face and the look of antique Themis. The frail young man of twenty bends the sturdy porter like a reed to his knees in the mire. The whole barricade gathers in a circle, speechless. Enjolras releases him, takes out his watch, and says 'Collect yourself. Think or pray. You have one minute.' Le Cabuc murmurs 'Mercy!' and stammers oaths. The minute passes; Enjolras pockets his watch, grasps him by the hair as he shrieks and coils at his knees, puts the muzzle to his ear, and fires. Many turn their heads away. He spurns the corpse with his foot: 'Throw that outside.' Three men fling the body, still twitching, over the little barricade into the Rue Mondétour.

Enjolras tells the citizens that what that man did was frightful and what he has done is horrible: he killed, therefore Enjolras killed him; insurrection must have its discipline, assassination is more of a crime here than anywhere since they are the priests of the Republic under the eyes of the Revolution, so he tried the man and condemned him, and has judged himself also, and they will soon see to what he has condemned himself. Combeferre cries 'We will share thy fate.' Enjolras adds that necessity is a monster of the old world named Fatality, that the law of progress is for Fatality to vanish before Fraternity, that he pronounces and glorifies the word love even at this bad moment, that he uses death but hates it, and that the day will come when the earth beams and the human race loves: 'it is in order that it may come that we are about to die.' He stands in marble immobility; Jean Prouvaire and Combeferre press hands and watch him with admiration mixed with compassion, executioner and priest, crystal and rock.

Hugo adds that when the bodies were searched at the morgue after the action a police agent's card was found on Le Cabuc, and that he himself held the 1832 report on it in 1848. A strange but probably well-founded police tradition says Le Cabuc was Claquesous; from Le Cabuc's death there was no more question of Claquesous, who left no trace of his disappearance, his life all shadows and his end night. While the barricade is still under the emotion of this swift trial, Courfeyrac again notices the small young man who had asked him for Marius that morning, who has come by night to join the insurgents with a bold and reckless air.

title: From the Rue Plumet to the Quartier Saint-Denis
summary: The voice summoning him to the barricade sounds to Marius like destiny offering death. Armed with Javert's pistols, he crosses Paris from the lit shops of the Rue de Rivoli, through the dense silent crowd and the army's bivouacs near the Halles, into the black, deserted insurgent quarter, passing an abandoned barricade, the omnibus's two white horses, and a stray bullet that pierces a barber's basin above his head.
details: The voice through the twilight has the effect of the voice of destiny: Marius wished to die, and a hand in the darkness offers the key to the tomb. Mad with grief after two months of youth and love, he says 'I will go', sets out at a rapid pace, and finds himself opportunely armed with Javert's pistols. The young man he thought he glimpsed has vanished.

He takes the boulevard, the Esplanade and bridge of the Invalides, the Champs-Élysées and the Place Louis XV to the Rue de Rivoli, where shops are open, gas burns under the arcades, women shop and people eat ices, and only a few post-chaises gallop from the hotels. Through the Passage Delorme into the Rue Saint-Honoré the shops are shut but merchants chat at their doors and windows are lit; cavalry stands on the Place du Palais-Royal. Further on the lights thin, the crowd thickens, and a dull deep murmur rises from people who do not speak. Near the Arbre-Sec fountain stand motionless gloomy groups; at the Rue des Prouvaires the crowd no longer walks but forms a solid block of blouses and caps whispering in the dark, and beyond it no window is lit, only lanterns hanging like red stars casting spider shadows, and the gleam of bayonets and bivouacking troops. There the rabble ends and the army begins.

Marius wills with the will of a man who hopes no more. He threads the throng, passes the bivouac, shuns patrols and sentinels, circles by the Rue de Béthisy towards the Halles; at the Rue des Bourdonnais the lanterns stop. Beyond the troops he enters something startling: no passer-by, no soldier, no light, a chill, each street like a cellar. Someone runs past him unseen. In what he judges the Rue de la Poterie he stumbles on an overturned wagon and scattered paving-stones, a barricade begun and abandoned, and climbs over. Something white ahead becomes two white horses, the omnibus horses Bossuet unharnessed that morning, straying all day with the patience of brutes. Near the Rue du Contrat-Social a shot from nowhere whistles past and pierces a brass shaving-dish hanging over a hairdresser's shop, a dish still to be seen there in 1848. After that he meets nothing; the whole route is like a descent of black steps, and he presses on.

title: An Owl’s View of Paris
summary: Hugo imagines Paris that night from above: the old Halles quarter a black cavity where every lit window has drawn a shot, with only the towers of Saint-Jacques and Saint-Merry rising from the dark, ringed by the swelling gleam of bayonets and artillery drawing in around it. Both sides know everything must be decided by the next day; the Saint-Merry tocsin wails under a black sky, and far off the sombre voice of the people roars.
details: A being hovering over Paris that night with an owl's wing would have seen the whole old quarter of the Halles, a city within a city threaded by the Rues Saint-Denis and Saint-Martin, as an enormous dark cavity in the centre of Paris. Lanterns broken and windows shut, the insurrection's invisible police keep order, that is, night: at dusk every window with a candle received a shot, so that nothing stirs and the houses hold only fright, mourning and stupor. Here and there indistinct gleams betray a barricade; above the lake of funereal obscurity rise the tower of Saint-Jacques, the church of Saint-Merry and a few more giants that night makes phantoms. All round, where street lamps still burn, the observer would see the metallic gleam of swords and bayonets, the rumble of artillery and silent battalions swelling minute by minute: a formidable girdle slowly tightening round the insurrection.
