The invested quarter is a monstrous cavern full of traps, where those who enter shiver before those who wait and those who wait shudder before those who come. Nothing more is to be hoped for but the lightning of guns and the abrupt apparition of death, where and when no one knows. Government and insurrection, National Guard and popular societies, bourgeois and uprising are groping towards contact; for one side to advance is death and no one thinks of retreat, for the other to remain is death and no one thinks of flight. All must be ended tomorrow: the insurrection must prove itself a revolution or a skirmish, and every bourgeois feels it. The only sound is the tocsin of Saint-Merry, as heartrending as a death rattle and menacing as a curse.

Nature accords with men: the stars have gone, heavy clouds fill the horizon, and a black sky rests on the dead streets like a winding-sheet over a tomb. While a battle still wholly political prepares, youth and the schools in the name of principles against the middle classes in the name of interests, far outside the fatal quarter, in the depths of wretched old Paris beneath the splendour of happy Paris, the sombre voice of the people gives a dull roar, a voice composed of the roar of the brute and the word of God, from below like the lion and from on high like the thunder.

title: The Extreme Edge
summary: Guided by the red glow of the torch, Marius creeps through the Rue des Prêcheurs to the elbow of the Rue Mondétour and looks into the interior of the barricade, ten fathoms away. There he sits on a post and thinks of his father: civil war seems a desecration of Colonel Pontmercy's sword, until he reasons that there is only just and unjust war and that the monarchy is itself a foreigner. Above the barricade he makes out the dead porter's head still staring from its window.
details: The Halles are calmer, darker and more motionless than the surrounding streets, as if the peace of the sepulchre had spread from earth to sky. A red glow on the tall roofs at the Saint-Eustache end of the Rue de la Chanvrerie is the torch of the Corinthe barricade. Marius follows it to the Marché-aux-Poirées, enters the dark mouth of the Rue des Prêcheurs unseen by the insurgents' sentinel at the far end, and on tiptoe reaches the elbow of the short fragment of the Rue Mondétour that Enjolras left as his only link to the outside. From the corner of the last house he sees light on the pavement, a bit of the wine-shop, a flickering lamp within a shapeless wall, and men crouching with guns on their knees, ten fathoms off: the interior of the barricade. The houses on his right hide the rest.

He has one step more to take. Instead he sits on a post, folds his arms, and thinks of his father: Colonel Pontmercy, who guarded France's frontier under the Republic and touched Asia's under Napoleon, who saw Genoa, Madrid, Vienna, Moscow, grew grey in discipline, and came home after twenty years scarred, smiling and pure as a child, having done everything for France and nothing against her. Marius tells himself his own hour has struck, that he too will run to meet bullets and seek death, and that his field of battle is the street and his war is civil war. He shudders. He thinks of his father's sword, sold by his grandfather to a dealer, and decides it did well to flee: coming from Marengo and Friedland it would not go to the Rue de la Chanvrerie, would have scorched his hands rather than wound its country's side; his grandfather was its true guardian. He weeps bitterly.

Yet what can he do? He cannot live without Cosette; he gave her his word he would die; she left without a word or letter though she knew his address, so she no longer loves him. Should he slink away after peeping in, abandon the friends expecting him, a handful against an army, and make patriotism the pretext for cowardice? His father's ghost would beat him with the flat of his sword and shout 'March on, you poltroon!' Then a splendid rectification comes over his mind, the clear sight that nearness to death gives. Why should his father be indignant? There are cases where insurrection rises to the dignity of duty. This is no longer sacred territory but a holy idea; France bleeds but liberty smiles. All war between men is war between brothers; there is only just and unjust war, and war is a disgrace only when it assassinates right and progress. Washington's sword need not disown Camille Desmoulins's pike. Street war was the war of Ambiorix and Pelagius against the foreigner, and the monarchy is a foreigner, divine right a stranger: driving out the tyrant or the English is the same reconquest of one's own territory. After philosophy, action; after Diderot, Danton. Louis Philippe is a good king, like Louis XVI, but principles are not parcelled out, and when the master falls in France he falls everywhere. To conquer at Austerlitz is grand; to take the Bastille is immense.

Hugo notes the soul's strange aptitude for cold reasoning in the most violent extremity, the thread of the syllogism floating unbroken in the storm. Dejected but resolute, still shuddering, Marius lets his glance stray into the barricade, where the insurgents talk low in the quasi-silence of the last stage of expectation. Overhead, at a small third-floor window, he sees a spectator who seems singularly attentive: the porter killed by Le Cabuc, his livid astonished face, bristling hair, fixed eyes and gaping mouth bent over the street as if the dead were surveying those about to die, a long trail of blood descending in reddish threads from the window to the first floor.

title: The Flag: Act First
summary: At ten o'clock Gavroche's warning song announces the troops. He bounds in, seizes Javert's gun, and forty-three insurgents kneel at the crest while Feuilly's six man the windows of Corinthe. A measured tread approaches in the dark, a voice calls 'Who goes there?', Enjolras answers 'The French Revolution!', and a volley cuts down the flagstaff and wounds several men. Enjolras asks who will plant the flag again, and no one answers.
details: Nothing has come yet when ten strikes from Saint-Merry. Enjolras and Combeferre sit with their carbines near the outlet of the large barricade, listening. Out of the dismal calm a clear, gay young voice from the direction of the Rue Saint-Denis sings a mocking verse about his friend Bugeaud's gendarmes and the suburbs in their blue capotes, to the tune of 'By the Light of the Moon', ending in a cock's crow. 'That is Gavroche,' says Enjolras; 'He is warning us,' says Combeferre. A hasty rush, and Gavroche climbs over the omnibus into the barricade, breathless: 'My gun! Here they are!' Enjolras offers his carbine; Gavroche wants a big gun, and seizes Javert's. Two sentinels fall back with him; the vidette of the Rue des Prêcheurs stays at his post, so nothing is coming from the Halles side.

Each man takes his position. Forty-three insurgents, among them Enjolras, Combeferre, Courfeyrac, Bossuet, Joly, Bahorel and Gavroche, kneel inside the large barricade with heads level with its crest and gun-barrels laid on the stones as in loopholes; six under Feuilly man the windows of the two storeys of Corinthe. Then a sound of footsteps, measured, heavy and numerous, comes from the direction of Saint-Leu, approaching without halt with a tranquil and terrible continuity, like the stone tread of the Commander's statue multiplied into a legion. It stops. Many men seem to breathe at the end of the street, and in the dense dark a multitude of fine metallic threads moves like the phosphorescence under closed eyelids: bayonets and gun-barrels catching the torch's distant reflection.

A pause, as if both sides waited. Then a sinister voice, the gloom itself speaking, shouts 'Who goes there?' and guns click into position. Enjolras answers in a haughty, vibrating tone: 'The French Revolution!' 'Fire!' A flash empurples the house-fronts like a furnace door flung open and shut; a fearful detonation bursts on the barricade. The red flag falls, the staff cut at the very tip of the omnibus pole; bullets ricochet from cornices into the barricade and wound several men. The impression is freezing: they have an entire regiment at least to deal with. Courfeyrac shouts not to waste powder but to wait till they are in the street; Enjolras says above all they must raise the flag, and picks it up where it fell at his feet. Outside, ramrods clatter as the troops reload. Enjolras asks who has a bold heart to plant the flag on the barricade again. No one answers: to climb it now is simply death, and even Enjolras feels a thrill. He repeats: 'Does no one volunteer?'

title: The Flag: Act Second
summary: Father Mabeuf, who has sat silent behind the counter since the barricade was built, rises at Enjolras's appeal, takes the flag from his hands and slowly climbs the barricade while the insurgents cry 'Off with your hats!' and take him for a member of the Convention. He waves the flag shouting 'Long live the Republic!', is ordered to retire, repeats the cry, and falls dead under the second volley. Enjolras kisses his brow and holds up his bullet-riddled coat: 'This is our flag now.'
details: No one has paid attention to Father Mabeuf since they reached Corinthe. He has sat behind the taproom counter, retreated into himself, not hearing Courfeyrac and the others who begged him to withdraw, his lips moving as if answering someone only when no one spoke to him. For hours he has kept one attitude, fists on knees, head thrust forward as if gazing over a precipice. When the men took their posts, only he and a single insurgent guarding Javert with a drawn sword remained in the taproom. The shock of the volley wakes him; he crosses the room, and at the instant Enjolras repeats 'Does no one volunteer?' the old man appears on the threshold. A shout goes up: 'It is the voter! It is the member of the Convention! It is the representative of the people!' He probably does not hear.

He walks straight to Enjolras, who recoils in amazement as the old man tears the flag from him, and since no one dares stop or help him, this man of eighty with shaking head and firm foot slowly climbs the paving-stone steps of the barricade. All around cry 'Off with your hats!' At every step his white hair, decrepit face, bald wrinkled brow and open mouth, his aged arm upholding the red banner, rise through the gloom enlarged in the bloody light of the torch, and the bystanders think they see the spectre of '93 rising from the earth with the flag of terror. On the last step, erect on the pile before twelve hundred invisible guns, he seems more powerful than death, and the whole barricade takes on a supernatural, colossal form. In the silence he waves the flag and shouts: 'Long live the Revolution! Long live the Republic! Fraternity! Equality! and Death!'

A low rapid whisper is heard from the far end of the street, probably the commissary of police making the legal summons; then the piercing voice shouts 'Retire!' Mabeuf, pale and haggard, eyes lit with the mournful flame of aberration, raises the flag above his head and repeats 'Long live the Republic!' 'Fire!' A second discharge rains on the barricade. The old man falls on his knees, rises, drops the flag and falls backwards full length on the pavement with outstretched arms, rivulets of blood beneath him, his pale sad face gazing at the sky. The insurgents, seized by an emotion that makes them forget to defend themselves, approach the body with awe.

'What men these regicides were!' says Enjolras. Courfeyrac whispers in his ear that this man was anything rather than a regicide: he knew him, his name was Father Mabeuf, he does not know what was the matter with him today, but he was a brave blockhead; just look at his head. 'The head of a blockhead and the heart of a Brutus,' Enjolras answers, and raises his voice: this is the example the old give to the young; they hesitated and he came, they drew back and he advanced; he has had a long life and a magnificent death, and each must defend this dead old man as he would his living father, so that his presence renders the barricade impregnable. A murmur of gloomy assent follows. Enjolras lifts the old man's head, kisses his brow, removes his coat with tender care, shows everyone the bloody holes in it, and says: 'This is our flag now.'

title: Gavroche Would Have Done Better to Accept Enjolras’ Carbine
summary: While Mabeuf's body is carried into the taproom past Javert, to whom Enjolras promises his turn presently, Gavroche alone stays on guard and shouts a warning: Municipal Guards are already climbing the barricade. Bahorel kills the first and is killed by the second's bayonet, Courfeyrac is thrown down, and a giant guardsman raises his bayonet over Gavroche, whose borrowed gun is not loaded. Two shots drop both guardsmen: Marius has entered the barricade.
details: They throw Widow Hucheloup's long black shawl over Father Mabeuf, make a litter of six guns, and carry him bareheaded with solemn slowness to the big table in the taproom, wholly absorbed in the sacred task and forgetting their peril. As the corpse passes Javert, still impassive at his post, Enjolras says to the spy: 'It will be your turn presently!'

Little Gavroche alone has not left his post. He thinks he sees men stealthily approaching, and shouts 'Look out!' Courfeyrac, Enjolras, Jean Prouvaire, Combeferre, Joly, Bahorel, Bossuet and the rest run tumultuously out of the wine-shop, almost too late: a glistening density of bayonets undulates above the barricade, and tall Municipal Guards are coming in, some striding over the omnibus, others through the cut, driving the urchin before them, who retreats but does not flee. It is the moment when the flood reaches the top of the levee; a second more and the barricade is taken.

Bahorel dashes at the first guard to enter and kills him with a blow of his gun; the second kills Bahorel with his bayonet. Another has already thrown down Courfeyrac, who is shouting 'Follow me!' The largest of all, a colossus, marches on Gavroche with fixed bayonet. The child levels Javert's huge gun resolutely at the giant and pulls the trigger: nothing. Javert's gun was not loaded. The guardsman laughs and raises his bayonet over the child. Before it touches him the gun slips from the soldier's grasp and he falls on his back with a bullet in the centre of his forehead; a second bullet strikes the guard who assaulted Courfeyrac full in the breast and lays him on the pavement. This is the work of Marius, who has just entered the barricade.

title: The Barrel of Powder
summary: Drawn in by Mabeuf's death, Bahorel's fall and the child in danger, Marius has fired both pistols, saving Gavroche and Courfeyrac. As a soldier aims at him, the young workman in velvet trousers puts a hand over the muzzle and falls with the shot. The troops crown the barricade; both sides fire point-blank; then Marius appears with a torch over the broken barrel of powder and threatens to blow up the barricade and himself with it, and the assailants flee.
details: Concealed in the turn of the Rue Mondétour, Marius has watched the first phase shuddering and irresolute, but cannot long resist the call of the abyss: the imminent peril, the death of M. Mabeuf, that melancholy enigma, Bahorel killed, Courfeyrac shouting 'Follow me!', the threatened child, friends to succour or avenge. He flings himself in with his two pistols, saving Gavroche with the first shot and delivering Courfeyrac with the second. Amid the shots the assailants, Municipal Guards, soldiers of the line and suburban National Guards, climb the entrenchment and cover two-thirds of it, but hesitate to leap into the dark enclosure as into a lion's den, the torch lighting only their bayonets, bearskins and angry faces.

Marius, weaponless, has flung away his discharged pistols, but has seen the barrel of powder by the taproom door. As he half turns towards it a soldier takes aim at him. A hand is laid over the muzzle: someone has darted forward, the young workman in velvet trousers. The shot goes through the hand and perhaps through the workman too, who falls, but the ball misses Marius, who entering the taproom barely registers the levelled gun, the hand that blocked it and the report; in such moments everything vacillates and one pauses for nothing.

The insurgents rally. Enjolras shouts not to fire at random; most climb to the first-floor windows and attics commanding the assailants, while the most determined, Enjolras, Courfeyrac, Jean Prouvaire and Combeferre, set their backs to the rear houses, unsheltered, facing the soldiers crowning the barricade, so close they could talk without raising their voices. An officer in a gorget extends his sword: 'Lay down your arms!' 'Fire!' answers Enjolras. Both volleys go off at once and all vanishes in acrid smoke; when it clears both sides are thinned but in place, reloading in silence. Then a thundering voice: 'Be off with you, or I'll blow up the barricade!'

Marius has seized the barrel of powder, slipped through the smoke to the cage of paving-stones holding the torch, torn out the torch, set the barrel in its place and thrust the stones under it, staving it in, all in the time it takes to stoop and rise. Now he stands with one foot on the stones and the torch in his hand, his face lit by fatal resolution, lowering the flame towards the broken barrel, while guards, officers and soldiers huddled at the far end of the barricade stare at him: Marius on that barricade after the octogenarian, the young revolution after the apparition of the old. A sergeant says: 'Blow up the barricade, and yourself with it!' 'And myself also,' Marius answers, and drops the torch towards the powder. But the barrier is already empty: the assailants have abandoned their dead and wounded and fled pell-mell into the night. The barricade is free.

title: End of the Verses of Jean Prouvaire
summary: The insurgents embrace Marius, and Enjolras names him chief. The wounded are laid on the widow's mattresses, the three women are found hiding in the cellar, and the roll-call shows Jean Prouvaire missing, evidently a prisoner. As Combeferre proposes to exchange Javert for him, a voice at the end of the street shouts 'Long live France! Long live the future!', a shot rings out, and Enjolras tells Javert: 'Your friends have just shot you.'
details: All flock round Marius; Courfeyrac flings himself on his neck and says that but for him he would be dead, Gavroche that he would have been gobbled up. Marius asks where the chief is. 'You are he!' says Enjolras. The furnace in Marius's brain has become a whirlwind: his two luminous months, Cosette lost, the barricade, M. Mabeuf killed for the Republic, himself the leader of the insurgents, all seem a nightmare he must make an effort to believe real. In this mist he does not recognise Javert, bound to his post, who has not moved his head during the attack and watches the revolt with the resignation of a martyr and the majesty of a judge; Marius has not even seen him.

The assailants do not stir, swarming at the end of the street but not venturing in, awaiting orders or reinforcements. Sentinels are posted; medical students among the insurgents tend the wounded. All the tables except the two for lint and cartridges and the one bearing Father Mabeuf are thrown onto the barricade and replaced by mattresses from the beds of the widow Hucheloup and her servants, on which the wounded are laid. The three women of Corinthe, whom no one could find, turn up hidden in the cellar.

A poignant emotion clouds the joy of the cleared barricade. The roll is called: one man is missing, one of the dearest and most valiant, Jean Prouvaire. He is not among the wounded nor the dead; he is evidently a prisoner. Combeferre says to Enjolras, near Javert's post: they have our friend, we have their agent; are you set on the death of that spy? 'Yes, but less so than on the life of Jean Prouvaire.' Combeferre proposes to tie his handkerchief to his cane and go as a flag of truce to offer the exchange. Enjolras lays a hand on his arm: 'Listen.' At the end of the street there is a clash of arms, and a manly voice shouts 'Vive la France! Long live France! Long live the future!' They recognise Prouvaire's voice. A flash, a report, silence. 'They have killed him,' cries Combeferre. Enjolras looks at Javert and says: 'Your friends have just shot you.'

title: The Agony of Death After the Agony of Life
summary: Inspecting the deserted little barricade, Marius hears his name breathed from the ground: it is Éponine, in men's clothes, dying of the bullet that passed through her hand and out through her back when she blocked the gun aimed at him. Lying with her head on his knees, she confesses she led him here so they might die together, tells him the singing gamin is her brother, gives him a letter she had kept from him, asks for a kiss on her brow when she is dead, says she believes she was a little in love with him, and dies.
details: Since barricades are almost always attacked from the front, all attention is on the grand barricade; but Marius thinks of the little one and finds it deserted, guarded only by the fire-pot trembling between the stones, the Mondétour lane and its branches profoundly calm. As he withdraws he hears his name pronounced feebly in the dark, in the voice that called him two hours earlier through the gate in the Rue Plumet, now no more than a breath. 'At your feet,' it says. He sees a form dragging itself along the pavement: a blouse, torn velvet trousers, bare feet, what looks like a pool of blood, and a pale lifted head asking whether he does not recognise her. 'Éponine.' It is that unhappy child, dressed as a man.

She says she is dying. He cries that he will carry her inside to be tended and tries to lift her; she gives a feeble cry, and shows him a black hole in the middle of her hand. 'Did you see a gun aimed at you?' 'Yes, and a hand stopping it.' 'It was mine.' Marius calls it madness and says one does not die of a pierced hand; she answers that the bullet went through her hand and out through her back, that moving her is useless, and that he can care for her better than any surgeon by sitting beside her on the stone. He obeys; she lays her head on his knees and says she no longer suffers. Without looking at him she admits it puzzled her that he entered that garden, stupidly, since she herself showed him the house; then, with a heartrending smile: 'You thought me ugly, didn't you?'

She tells him he is lost, that no one can get out of the barricade now, that it was she who led him here and she counts on his dying, and yet when she saw them aiming at him she put her hand on the muzzle, because she wanted to die before him. After the bullet she dragged herself here unseen and waited for him, biting her blouse with the pain. She recalls the day she looked in his mirror and the day on the boulevard by the washerwomen when the birds sang and she refused his hundred sous, and hopes he picked up the coin. 'Oh! How happy I am! Everyone is going to die.' Blood spurts from a second hole in her breast under her pressed hand. Gavroche's cock-crow rings out as he loads his gun on a table singing a song about Lafayette and the gendarme; she listens and murmurs 'It is he. My brother is here. He must not see me. He would scold me.' Marius, who has been thinking bitterly of the duties to the Thénardiers his father bequeathed him, asks who her brother is: that little fellow, the one singing.

She says she does not wish to play him a trick: she has a letter for him in her pocket, which she was told to post and kept, not wanting it to reach him, but perhaps he would be angry with her when they meet again presently. She puts his hand in her blouse pocket; he takes the letter, and she makes a sign of contentment. For her trouble she asks a promise: to give her a kiss on her brow when she is dead; she will feel it. Her head drops on his knees and her eyes close; he thinks her gone. Then she opens them, with the sombre depth of death in them, and says in a voice that already seems to come from another world: 'And by the way, Monsieur Marius, I believe that I was a little bit in love with you.' She tries to smile once more and expires.

title: Gavroche as a Profound Calculator of Distances
summary: Marius kisses Éponine's brow and reads the letter: Cosette writes on 4 June that her father is taking her that evening to 7 Rue de l'Homme Armé and to England in a week. Hugo explains that Éponine was the warning-bearer on the Champ-de-Mars, the 'young workman' Cosette entrusted with the note, and the voice at the Rue Plumet gate, all to drag Marius into death with her. Marius writes a farewell to Cosette and a note asking that his body be carried to his grandfather, and sends Gavroche off with the letter; Gavroche, meaning to be back before the barricade falls, sets off at once.
details: Marius keeps his promise and kisses the livid, sweat-beaded brow, a pensive farewell to an unhappy soul and no infidelity to Cosette. He feels at once that the letter is an event of weight, lays Éponine gently down, and reads it by a taproom candle. It is a small note sealed with a woman's care, addressed to Monsieur Marius Pontmercy at M. Courfeyrac's, 16 Rue de la Verrerie: her father insists on leaving immediately; this evening they will be at No. 7 Rue de l'Homme Armé; in a week they will be in England. Signed Cosette, 4 June. Such was the innocence of their love that Marius did not even know her handwriting.

Hugo explains in a few words. Since the night of 3 June Éponine had two aims: to defeat her father and the ruffians at the Rue Plumet, and to separate Marius and Cosette. She swapped rags with a young scamp who found it amusing to dress as a woman, and in man's clothes conveyed to Jean Valjean on the Champ-de-Mars the warning 'Leave your house.' Valjean came home and told Cosette they would leave that evening for the Rue de l'Homme Armé with Toussaint and be in London next week. Cosette, overwhelmed, wrote a couple of lines to Marius, but could not post them herself and dared not trust Toussaint, who would show them to M. Fauchelevent; through the fence she saw the 'young workman' prowling, called to him, and gave him five francs and the letter to carry at once. Éponine pocketed it. On the 5th she went to Courfeyrac's asking for Marius, not to deliver it but 'to see'; when Courfeyrac said they were going to the barricades, the idea flashed on her to fling herself into that death and thrust Marius into it too. She followed, made sure of the place, then went to the Rue Plumet, certain he would come at dusk since he had had no warning, and sent him the summons in his friends' name, counting on his despair at finding Cosette gone. She died with the tragic joy of jealous hearts who say 'No one shall have him!'

Marius covers Cosette's letter with kisses: so she loves him. For a moment he thinks he ought not to die now; then he reflects that she is going to England and his grandfather refuses the marriage, so nothing in their fates is changed, and despair returns. Two duties remain: to tell Cosette of his death with a last farewell, and to save from the coming catastrophe that poor child, Éponine's brother and Thénardier's son. He tears a leaf from his pocketbook and writes in pencil that their marriage was impossible, his grandfather refused, neither of them has a fortune, he hastened to her and she was gone, he keeps his promise and dies, he loves her, and when she reads this his soul will be near her and she will smile; he folds it unsealed and addresses it to Mademoiselle Cosette Fauchelevent, 7 Rue de l'Homme Armé. On the first page of the pocketbook he writes: 'My name is Marius Pontmercy. Carry my body to my grandfather, M. Gillenormand, Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire, No. 6, in the Marais.'

He calls Gavroche, who runs up devotedly, saying that but for Marius he would have been done for, and asks him to take the letter, leave the barricade instantly, and deliver it tomorrow morning to Mademoiselle Cosette at M. Fauchelevent's. Gavroche scratches his ear: meanwhile the barricade will be taken and he will not be there. Marius says it will not be attacked before daybreak nor taken before noon, and that tomorrow will be too late because the streets will be blockaded. Gavroche stands undecided, then snatches the letter with a birdlike movement, says 'All right', and runs off through the Mondétour lane. His unspoken idea: it is barely midnight, the Rue de l'Homme Armé is not far, he will deliver the letter at once and be back in time.

title: A Drinker Is a Babbler
summary: On the evening of 4 June Jean Valjean moved Cosette and Toussaint to the Rue de l'Homme Armé with only 'the inseparable' valise, and by the next evening the quiet street has restored his serenity. Then, in the slanting mirror over the sideboard, he reads the reversed imprint of Cosette's note to Marius on her open blotting-book. The light of his life goes out; he guesses at once that the man is the prowler of the Luxembourg, finds hatred in his heart, asks Toussaint where the fighting is, and goes to sit bareheaded on the post at his door as night falls.
details: Hugo turns from the convulsions of the city to the insurrection of a soul: Jean Valjean, at that very moment, is on the brink of his own obscure revolution. On the evening before 5 June he installed himself with Cosette and Toussaint in the Rue de l'Homme Armé. Cosette had resisted for the first time in their life together, objections on one side and inflexibility on the other; the stranger's 'Leave your house' had made him peremptory, convinced he was traced. They arrived without a word, he too uneasy to notice her sadness, she too sad to notice his unease. He brought Toussaint, who is not curious ('I do my work; the rest is no affair of mine'), and carried away only the little embalmed valise Cosette calls 'the inseparable', since full trunks need porters and porters are witnesses; Cosette brought only her portfolio and blotting-book. They left at dusk, which gave Cosette time to write her note, and went to bed in silence in a second-floor back apartment of two bedrooms, a dining-room and kitchen, with a garret for Toussaint.

Confidence returns as foolishly as it goes. The narrow, silent old street, barred to carriages by a beam, soothes him; he sleeps well with the inseparable beside him and wakes almost gay, finding the hideous dining-room charming. Cosette keeps to her room all day with broth and a headache, glances at a cold chicken at five out of deference, and shuts herself up again. Valjean eats a wing with appetite, barely hears Toussaint stammer that they are fighting in Paris, and paces the room growing serene, arranging in his mind a few months in London with Cosette, who is his nation and suffices for his happiness; the idea that he might not suffice for hers does not even present itself. Then his glance meets, in the inclined mirror over the sideboard, four lines: 'My dearest, alas! my father insists on our setting out immediately. We shall be this evening in the Rue de l'Homme Armé, No. 7. In a week we shall be in England. Cosette. June 4th.' Cosette had left her blotting-book open on the sideboard at the page where she dried the note she gave the young workman; the mirror rights the reversed imprint.

He reads it again and does not believe it; examines the scrawl on the blotter, finds no sense in it, and breathes with foolish relief; then looks at the mirror again and understands. He totters into the old armchair, head drooping, telling himself the light of the world is eclipsed forever and Cosette has written that to someone, and hears his soul give a dull roar in the gloom. Chance has brought Marius's letter to him before Marius has received Cosette's. Hugo says that of all his trials this is the most terrible, the loss of the beloved being; that Valjean loves Cosette as a father, but a father forged from grandfather, son, brother and husband, with even a mother included, and that into this paternity the widowhood of his life has let in every shade of love. Seeing her slip from him like a cloud, seeing that another is the goal of her heart and he is nothing but her father, the 'I' in this man's abyss howls, and he feels the immense reawakening of egotism. He recognises the precipice he feared last summer: he is no longer on its brink but at its bottom, and had fallen without perceiving it.

His instinct does not hesitate: putting together dates, blushes and pallors, he says 'It is he', and strikes on the unknown prowler of the Luxembourg, that idler of romance, that coward who made eyes at a girl with a loving father beside her. And he, the regenerated man who laboured so long to turn all misery into love, looks into his breast and sees a spectre: Hate. Toussaint enters; he asks in what quarter the fighting is, and she says towards Saint-Merry. Five minutes later, by a movement he is hardly conscious of, he is in the street, sitting bareheaded on the stone post at his door, seeming to listen. Night has come.

title: The Street Urchin an Enemy of Light
summary: Jean Valjean sits frozen on his doorpost as Saint-Paul strikes eleven and the two volleys sound from the Halles. Gavroche arrives in the Rue de l'Homme Armé looking for No. 7, smashes the street lantern, refuses a five-franc piece as a bribe and then accepts it for his mother, and lets slip that he carries a letter from the barricade for Mademoiselle Cosette. Valjean claims to be the person it is for, takes the paper, and Gavroche flutters off breaking another lantern in the Rue du Chaume.
details: How long he sits there, whether he can still regain his footing in his conscience, he could not have said. The street is deserted; a few bourgeois hurry home; the lamplighter lights the lantern opposite No. 7 and goes. Valjean sits motionless as ice while alarm bells and uproar sound in the distance and the clock of Saint-Paul strikes eleven, for the tocsin is man and the hour is God. Then a brusque report from the direction of the Halles, and a second more violent, probably the attack on the Rue de la Chanvrerie barricade repulsed by Marius; he starts up, turns towards the noise, falls back on the post with folded arms and sinking head, and resumes his gloomy dialogue with himself.

Footsteps: by the lantern-light he sees a young, livid, beaming face. Gavroche has arrived in the Rue de l'Homme Armé, staring up at the house-fronts and feeling the bolted doors and windows of five or six barricaded houses, then shrugging: 'Pardi!' Valjean, who a moment ago would have spoken to no one, feels impelled to ask what is the matter with him. 'The matter with me is that I am hungry. Little fellow yourself.' Valjean draws out a five-franc piece, but Gavroche has picked up a stone and noticed the lantern: they still have their lanterns here, which is disorderly, and he flings the stone and puts out the light, to cries from behind curtains that 'Ninety-three' has come again. He asks what that gigantic monument at the end of the street is, the Archives, and talks of crumbling its pillars into a barricade.

Valjean murmurs 'Poor creature, he is hungry' and lays the hundred-sou piece in his hand. Gavroche, who knows five-franc pieces only by hearsay, contemplates 'the tiger' in ecstasy, then holds it out again: he prefers to smash lanterns and cannot be bribed. 'Have you a mother?' 'More than you have, perhaps.' 'Well, keep the money for your mother!' Gavroche is touched, notices the man has no hat, which inspires confidence, pockets the coin, calls him a fine man, and asks whether he belongs in this street and where No. 7 is. Then he checks himself, fearing he has said too much. An idea flashes on Valjean: 'Are you the person who is bringing a letter that I am expecting?' 'You? You are not a woman.' 'The letter is for Mademoiselle Cosette, is it not?' 'Cosette. Yes, I believe that is the queer name.' Valjean says he is the person to whom it is to be delivered; Gavroche warns that then he must know it was sent from the barricade. 'Of course.'

Gavroche draws a paper folded in four from another pocket, salutes ('Respect for despatches. It comes from the Provisional Government'), holds it above his head and declares it is not a love letter but for the people, since men fight and respect the fair sex, decides the man has the air of an honest one, and hands it over, adding that he should make haste because Mamselle Cosette is waiting. Valjean asks whether the answer goes to Saint-Merry; Gavroche says he is making brioches, the letter comes from the barricade of the Rue de la Chanvrerie and he is going back there, and flutters away like an escaped bird into the dark. A few minutes later the crash of another lantern in the Rue du Chaume wakes the indignant bourgeois again.

title: While Cosette and Toussaint Are Asleep
summary: Jean Valjean creeps upstairs like a thief and reads Marius's note by candlelight, seeing only 'I die. When thou readest this, my soul will be near thee.' He feels a frightful inward joy: the man who stands between him and Cosette is going to his death of his own accord, and Valjean need only keep the note in his pocket. Then he grows gloomy, wakes the porter, and an hour later goes out armed, in full National Guard uniform, towards the markets.
details: Valjean goes into the house with Marius's letter, gropes up the stairs as pleased with the dark as an owl gripping its prey, shuts his door softly, listens to be sure Cosette and Toussaint are asleep, and plunges three or four matches into the lighter before his trembling hand gets a spark. What he has just done smacks of theft. He unfolds the paper. In violent emotion one does not read, one seizes on one point; in Marius's note to Cosette he sees only: 'I die. When thou readest this, my soul will be near thee.'

Before those two lines he is horribly dazzled, crushed by the change taking place within him, staring at the note with intoxicated amazement at that splendour, the death of a hated individual. He utters a frightful cry of inward joy. So it is all over; the catastrophe has come sooner than he dared hope; the being who obstructed his destiny is disappearing freely, willingly, through no fault of his. His fever calculates: perhaps he is dead already; no, the letter was meant to be read tomorrow morning, nothing has happened since the two discharges between eleven and midnight, the barricade will not be seriously attacked before daybreak; but it makes no difference, from the moment 'that man' is in this war he is caught in the gearing and cannot escape. Valjean feels delivered: he will be alone with Cosette again, the rivalry will cease, the future begin anew. He need only keep the note in his pocket; Cosette will never know what became of that man. 'What good fortune!'

Having said all this to himself, he becomes gloomy. Then he goes downstairs and wakes the porter. About an hour later Jean Valjean goes out in the complete costume of a National Guard, the uniform glimpsed earlier in Toussaint's packages, with a loaded gun and a cartridge-box full of cartridges which the porter has easily found in the neighbourhood, and strides off in the direction of the markets.

title: Gavroche’s Excess of Zeal
summary: On his way back Gavroche sings through the empty streets, tips a drunken Auvergnat out of his handcart to take it for the barricade, leaves a receipt signed 'Gavroche' in the man's waistcoat, and gallops off with it, rousing the National Guard post at the Royal Printing Establishment. Confronted by the sergeant, he answers with insults, launches the cart into his stomach, and escapes under a quarter-hour of blind musketry, worried only that the detour may make him late for the barricade.
details: After stoning the lantern in the Rue du Chaume, Gavroche enters the deserted Rue des Vieilles-Haudriettes and strikes up a long ditty with the refrain 'Où vont les belles filles, lon la', listing Atala, Mila, Agnès, Paméla, Suzette, Zéila, Lola, Jeanne and Stella, accompanied by grimaces that no one sees in the dark. He stops short at an 'ensemble' in a carriage doorway: a handcart with its shafts on the pavement and an Auvergnat errand-man asleep drunk inside it. 'We'll take the cart for the Republic, and leave the Auvergnat for the Monarchy.' Picturing how bully the cart would look on the barricade, he tugs the cart from behind and the man by the feet until the Auvergnat lies flat on the pavement still snoring, writes with a carpenter's red pencil a receipt, 'French Republic. Received thy cart. Gavroche', tucks it in the sleeper's waistcoat pocket, and sets off towards the Halles pushing the cart at a hard gallop with a glorious uproar.

This is perilous: there is a post of suburban National Guards at the Royal Printing Establishment. For an hour the boy's broken lanterns and bawled song have been the uproar of a fly in a bottle to that peaceable quarter, and the prudent sergeant has been listening; the mad rattle of the cart decides him to reconnoitre, muttering that there must be a whole band. Turning into the Rue des Vieilles-Haudriettes Gavroche comes face to face with a uniform, shako, plume and gun. 'Hullo, it's him. Good day, public order.' To the sergeant's repeated 'Where are you going, you rascal, rogue, villain, bandit, wretch?' Gavroche answers that he has not yet called him bourgeois so why insult him, that he must have been a man of wit yesterday but has degenerated this morning, that he should sell his hairs at a hundred francs apiece for five hundred francs, and finally, as the bayonet lowers, that he is going to fetch a doctor for his wife who is in labour. 'To arms!' shouts the sergeant.

The cart that betrayed him must now protect him: Gavroche launches it with all his might, it strikes the sergeant full in the stomach and tumbles him into the gutter as his gun goes off in the air. The post rushes out, the shot sets off a general random discharge, and the blind-man's-buff musketry lasts a quarter of an hour and kills several panes of glass. Gavroche, having retraced his steps at full speed, sits panting on the corner post of the Enfants-Rouges five or six streets away, thumbs his nose three times at the fusillade, and worries that he is losing his way and must take a roundabout route: 'If I only reach the barricade in season!' He runs on, picks up his ditty where he left it, with new verses about remaining bastilles and Charles X coming unstuck, and his voice dies away in the gloom. The cart is impounded and the drunken Auvergnat later harassed before the councils of war as an accomplice; the affair lingers in the Marais as 'The nocturnal attack by the post of the Royal Printing Establishment'.
